speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: COURTENAY-POWELL RIVER, B.C.-PROVISION OF SATELLITE STATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Approximately 15 months ago C.B.C. authorities announced their intention to proceed immediately with the construction of a satellite station of CBUT-Vancouver to serve the Courtenay-Powell River area. Inasmuch as there is no visible evidence of any progress toward the establishment of this station, can the minister inform me of the reason for the delay and when some action may be expected?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: COURTENAY-POWELL RIVER, B.C.-PROVISION OF SATELLITE STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sent me notice of this question yesterday. The fact that there was no question period yesterday enabled me to get the information from the corporation. I am advised as follows. On December 28, 1959, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation filed an application with the Department of Transport for authority to establish on channel 7 a satellite of CBUT-Vancouver to serve the Courtenay-Powell River area. It was referred to the board of broadcast governors by the Department of Transport on February 8, 1960, and was considered at the public hearing held in Toronto on March 14-18. The board announced their recommendation for approval on March 31, 1960.
The corporation is still awaiting the final authorization for establishment of this station from the Department of Transport. The delay is caused by a question of channel allocation being worked out internationally, and negotiations have been going on between the Department of Transport and the federal communications commission for some months. My last information is that a settlement of this question is to be expected shortly, an end which I desire very devoutly will be achieved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to answer the question of the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages). Would you kindly allow me, Mr. Speaker, to continue in English?
(Text):
I should like to make a brief statement, Mr. Speaker, on the new lending policy for which provision is made in the amendment to the National Housing Act passed by the house on November 25. The bill has received royal assent and appropriate regulations are now being submitted for approval by the governor in council.
In discussing the intent of the regulations I shall speak first only of loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The larger loans available under the new legislation and the higher maximum loans by regulation are, of course, immediately available to any eligible prospective borrower who cannot find accommodation from an approved lender. Furthermore, provided a request is made in writing prior to the date for adjustment of interest, that is the date on which monthly mortgage payments start to run, the more generous terms also apply to a home owner applicant or to a purchaser who has assumed the mortgage from a builder and to a builder at the time of the sale of houses financed by corporation loans.
To answer the question asked by the hon. member for Nipissing on Friday last, the

Inquiries of the Ministry higher loan and the new maximum loans by regulation will also be available in the case of any unsold house built by a builder and financed by a direct C.M.H.C. loan, even if the date for adjustment of interest has passed. The amendment also permits a longer period for repayment of a National Housing Act mortgage loan. This longer period, up to 35 years, will be available to a new borrower if he needs it to meet payments of principal, interest and taxes.
In the case of rental properties financed under the National Housing Act, the higher loan ratio and the new maximum by regulation will also be available, again provided the date for adjustment of interest has not been reached.
The new terms to which I have referred also apply to insured loans made by the approved lenders, banks, life insurance companies, trust and loan companies. I cannot, of course, speak on the probable action to be taken by the approved lenders with respect to these terms, but the terms are available.

Vocational Training

subtopic: PRESENCE OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, December 2, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training and to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs of technical and vocational training undertaken under provincial authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs; to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons; to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and incidental matters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I rise to voice wholehearted support for this resolution, because I think if more attention had been paid to vocational training 10 years ago we should not have the unemployment which exists today.
The minister has told us that Canada has never trained enough manpower for her own needs; we have had to depend on immigration for our skilled labour, and I think we are doing the right thing now in emphasizing the need for more vocational training. In a speech made recently in Toronto Mr. Karl Scott, president of the Ford Company of Canada, warned that Canadians no longer enjoyed technological superiority in this world. Management, government, organized labour and the public in this country, he said, must recognize world competition and be prepared to face its threat and meet it. I think this particular resolution which the Minister of Labour has presented is one practical way of trying to meet world competition and overcome unemployment.
In the past few decades there have been many changes in our labour force and great shifts in our population. In 1900, 50 per cent of the workers in Canada were employed in agriculture. Today only 12 per cent are so employed. Then there is technology; new machinery is replacing manpower, and the time has come when men must learn new skills. Then again, more married women are working than ever before in Canada's history, except for the period during the war. There are now 77,000 married women collecting unemployment insurance.

Finally, our health standards have improved so much that more and more healthy pensioners are working either full time or part time. We have 368,000 unemployed, yet on reading our newspapers it is amazing to see how many advertisements there are for men and women with special skills to be employed at specific jobs. In developing this vocational training program I hope careful studies will be made of the kinds of skills and trades that are in demand today and in respect of which training should be undertaken. I hope the men and women concerned will be guided in this training so they may be fitted for these available jobs. It seems to me that this far-sighted project will do a great deal to combat not only seasonal unemployment but permanent unemployment also.
The minister has told us that 15 per cent of the unskilled workers are among the unemployed. I should like to see the Department of Labour send officials into Canadian schools, public schools and high schools, in order to give information about the jobs that are available. It could be that counsellors would not only provide information but would also spark ambition in boys and girls and inspire them to set out for certain goals. I feel that possibly one of the reasons so many young people are not going on to courses of higher education is that they do not know what to do. I think industry could well spend more time and energy in encouraging ambition in this way and in preaching the value of trades and skills. Millions of dollars are spent by industry in courting the consumer through public relations work. If some of this money were diverted to schools to encourage the ambition of young people to learn a trade or craft I believe it would be a fine investment in the future.
The hon. member for Halton spoke of the psychological problem with regard to vocational training, and said the dignity and importance of vocational training should be emphasized. I agree. I think for too long we have allowed technical training, as against university training, to become something of a second class proposition, and I believe it is a task of both government and industry to alter this situation. It seems to me that in a country such as Canada a fine craftsman is much more important than a bachelor of arts.
Moreover, to be idle can produce a demoralizing effect, especially upon young people. In studying the causes of today's unemployment, we find that high on the list is this large influx of young people. These are war babies who have come into the labour force. These young people came in during a very high wage economy. In their teens they

were often able to earn more in the summer months than 20 years ago their fathers were able to earn in six months. That situation has changed now. The young people who leave school too soon without adequate training are now among the unemployed. They are the ones who need and should be given this training.
There are two things I can say to the Minister of Labour, and I say them with the authority of observation in my own riding. In struggling with the problem of unemployment, which is such a great problem in Canada, the Minister of Labour is not alone. I hope it will hearten him to know that many segments of our private citizens are not only giving great thought to this problem but are trying to do something about it. For instance, I have noticed that in the schools in my riding of York-Humber a number of the teachers are laying great stress on the need for education and for training in specific fields, and are trying to persuade the students to take all the education they can possibly absorb before they leave school.
Then, too, private citizens have formed themselves into committees on things like winter works programs. There is one such committee in the town of Weston in my riding. It has been definitely established that this committee last year placed men and women in 158 jobs. That number of jobs in relation to more than 300,000 unemployed may not sound like too much, but if every small community should find 158 jobs for their citizens it would go a long way toward solving the unemployment problem.
The local council of women in Weston has concerned itself particularly with the training of young people. Research by this organization has disclosed, for instance, that in the motor mechanics field there is accommodation for 30,000 skilled workers in apprentice training, while only 6,000 are enrolled at the present time. Other disclosures and suggestions indicate that technology is going to demand higher skill from the new workers, that unemployment insurance should not be considered as a wage that has been earned but considered as a resource for persons who are genuinely unemployed, and that steps should be taken to make it necessary for applicants to take training in order to draw unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order. Would hon. members kindly lower their voices. Some hon. gentlemen have advised me that they are unable to hear the speaker.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I believe the Department of Labour should do a little educational work of its own in trying to make not only young people but all unemployed people have a
Vocational Training
feeling of training-mindedness. A recent survey has shown some discouraging results as to how many women would be willing to take courses if they were available. They have given several reasons for their unwillingness to participate in courses. In the first place they do not want to take courses because of a need for immediate financial returns. Second, they have home responsibilities. Third, some have insufficient educational background.
The other day Mr. William Thomson, director of employment services for the unemployment insurance commission in Ottawa, rather turned the penny over in regard to the subject of unemployment and employment. He said that Canada's chief employment problem today is not to find work for unskilled labour but to fill vacancies in professional and highly skilled categories.
I feel that this resolution is extremely welcome at this time, and I believe it to be a long-sighted project.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps before making my own remarks I may say how interested I was in those just made by the hon. member for York-Humber. I believe we can take it that the need for technical and vocational training has been fully established, and I propose to say practically nothing on that subject at this time.
I was struck by one of the remarks made by the Minister of Labour in introducing this resolution, when he pointed out that 35 per cent of our highly skilled technicians in this country came from abroad. I was also struck by the other convincing arguments that he made. As I say, I do not wish to speak on that. What I wish to do is put forward a word of caution, so to speak, although I am sure it is not really necessary, and say I believe that in stressing vocational education we must remember we are training not only technicians but citizens. We must therefore have an adequate amount of what I can only call collateral education in training people who will have to consider important questions and who will be deciding these questions by their votes later on.
There is one particular point I wish to make in this connection. If we confine ourselves entirely to technical and vocational education and do nothing to train citizens we may find that we have a number of good technicians with no sense of Canadian citizenship, who may drift to the United States. I feel it is during the period of education that we have to make them feel that Canada is worth-while living in. My own feeling is that they have to have some knowledge of Canadian history and institutions so they may develop a sense of Canadianism. On the other

Vocational Training
hand, I would have thought that the events of the last 40 years and the fact that we have had to play a part in two wars should have created a basis for a real Canadian patriotism.
Also, these people must have some knowledge of economics to understand the conditions under which their industry exists, both its strengths and weaknesses. Above all, I believe they have to be made feel that they are part of the show, that they have some interest as individuals, that they are not working solely for someone else. I remember hearing a wise remark made by the great Churchill when speaking of the background of English history. He said the great thing about us is that we are constantly bringing new people in and making them feel they are part of the show.
I personally feel that this is tremendously important. If we can make the rank and file of the industrial worker feel they are part of the show it will undoubtedly give them a different attitude. It will make them feel that they have both a responsibility and an opportunity. If they are going to have that feeling they must know something about the conditions of competition both at home and abroad. They must realize that over the long run industry can only pay what it earns.
Employers must also contribute to this knowledge to the end that labour may feel it is co-operating. In rowing terms, labour and management must "pull together", not "row jealous". They must learn to pull together instead of each trying to get ahead of the other.
I submit this is not impossible. The Prime Minister used wise words of admonition in saying that this is no time for people to be thinking exclusively of themselves. I am not entirely without experience in labour relations. When I was in business it fell to my lot on more than one occasion to represent the company with which I was associated as a receiver and manager in industry. I was in charge of running a steel plant for several years. I believe I can say we made friends of these people. It is perfectly true that the receiver is in an easier position than the ordinary manager. By reason of his appointment he is working for everybody. He is working to try to restore the business to health; he is working for the operatives, the shareholders, the bondholders, everybody. I can remember a hard-boiled American manufacturer at that time telling me that he had not too much sympathy for the working man. He thought there could be no sympathetic relationship.
I hope those days are past.
I heard of a case the other day which shows that where trouble is taken to present

the problem to the people in advance, they will be ready to co-operate. This was a case where a certain group of workmen in a plant were making a component of a product. The management discovered that they had reached the point in dealing with this group of workmen where it was costing more than a synthetic product which was available. They got this group together and told them the story. They make it perfectly clear, that by employing those men they were losing money. It became perfectly clear that to keep on working they would have to take less money, and they did. There was a real problem, and the manufacturer took the men into his confidence, show them the position and let them make the decision, and that was their decision.
I think myself, when we look at the competition in the world today, we do realize that special co-operation is necessary. I do not need to go further than the very able brief which the Ontario government presented to the Bladen automotive commission. This is quoted in an article in the Globe and Mail of October 26 last. I have read the brief, and I consider the summary in the Globe and Mail a fair one. I should like to read from it, because it seems to me to put the thing very clearly. The editorial says, referring to the brief:
It looks at the dilemma of all Canadian industry -high costs, high prices-and explains how Canadian industry got there.
The trouble began, essentially, when the war ended 15 years ago. There was then an unlimited demand for everything Canada's factories could produce; the gutted factories of Japan and Europe offered no competition. It was Canada's opportunity to exploit the misfortunes of other people, to get rich because of other people's poverty-and we seized the opportunity with both hands. Heedless of the future, never thinking that Japanese and European industry might come back, we treated ourselves to bigger profits, higher wages, shorter hours, a languid and luxurious way of life. Not only did we live right up to our means, but went beyond them by borrowing.
Now comes the day of reckoning. As the Ontario brief points out, the industries of Europe and Asia now "not only have modern, highly efficient equipment that matches our own, but substantially lower wage rates".
I read one more sentence. After quoting again from the brief the Globe and Mail editorial continues:
The main remedy rests not with the Canadian government, but with Canadian industry itself.
Then in the final paragraph I think there is a lesson for all of us. I should have said first that almost without exception the organizations which appeared before the commission asked the government to solve the unemployment problem by artificial measures of one sort or another, such as higher tariffs, bigger hand-outs, more subsidies, easier loans, higher wages, shorter hours, even peacetime

conscription for military service. I continue quoting from the Globe and Mail:
Judging from press reports, there was one word which nobody mentioned at the unemployment conference, one remedy which nobody proposed- work. Perhaps this four-letter word has, like other four-letter words, become offensive; perhaps like them, it is not to be found in the popular dictionary. We suggest it had better be reinstated in Canada, because it has been reinstated-often is deified-in most other parts of the world. Otherwise, to borrow a phrase from Mr. Frost, Canada will be "a sitting duck" not just for imports but for unemployment of a much deeper and deadlier nature than we have today.
May I say just a word about Japan. I was very interested the other day in talking to a friend of mine who had just come back from Japan. He said that the Japanese people are better than we are. I looked at him, and I found that what he meant was that they seemed to work with the feeling that they knew they were part of the show. They seemed to feel that they were working in their own interest, and it was in their interest to do their very best. That struck me as being very significant, very important.
I come now to Germany. Of course some people would be inclined to say, "Well, the Germans are amenable to discipline". I found on reading the International Labour Review that that does not seem to be the case. It appears, too, that in Germany there has been legislation making labour a part of the show, giving labour a very considerable say in management. I have not pursued it far enough to speak with detailed knowledge, but I suggest it is a matter that should be of interest to us all, and we should not ignore it.
I again say I do not think we should regard ourselves as having the world by the tail on a downhill pull. I recall some years ago speaking to an economist who had lately returned from Europe. He indicated the picture in Europe, where they have a tremendous amount of work going on, tremendous prosperity and so forth. I recall reading the last issue of the London Economist. I was rather surprised to find that they had a lot to say about the United States, which is apparently moaning about its affairs, and I was rather interested to see the Economist telling the United States not to be downhearted, that they were really all right.
Again coming back to the European situation, it may be that with the progress in Europe; with the astonishing progress made by the common market and the Six, which has succeeded beyond its expectations; with the possibility of injury for us by reason of their operations and by reason of Britain's need to adhere more to Europe, and by reason of what these. dangers mean, we should
Vocational Training
be taking the situation very seriously. In that connection I want to read just a short extract from a report made two or three years ago of a study conference called by the Duke of Edinburgh. Apparently they discussed the problems of industrial relations. The conference was called "Human Problems of Industrial Communities". The man who summed up the conference had this to say, and I shall read briefly:
Again and again groups reported that all the techniques of management-joint consultation, promotion schemes, bonus systems, welfare arrangements-are subordinate to one overriding demand- the demand for personal contact between manager and managed with an absolute sincerity of purpose and a recognition of the simple respect which one man owes to another as man to man.
I quote further where the report says:
That satisfaction, contentment and efficiency are so largely dependent on men and women being able to identify themselves clearly with the purpose and results of the businesses in which they work.
I am sure all will agree that is only good common sense, and I am sure it is a worthwhile objective for all of us. I hope I have not seemed to stray a long way from vocational training. In any event, if I have I am nearly through my wanderings. I do not think I have strayed, because these men who will receive training are going to be leaders in industry. They will not be merely technicians but will go on to become leaders in various ways, and their attitude can be of great importance.
I think it was the Duke of Wellington who said that in war, morale as against material rated ten to one. I do not suppose we would care to go quite that far with respect to industry, but we would be prepared to say that morale contributes an enormous amount, and that when it is there it makes a great deal of difference. In fact I could mention employers right in this house who I know have high morale among those working for them. The reason for this is very simple. It is because they have made clear to their employees that they care about them, that their welfare is close to the heart of the employer, and they are going to give them every chance and make them feel they are part of the show.
You may ask, does it need a miracle to produce this attitude? I would say not, while it is easy to say what shall be done; it is another thing to do it. All that is needed is that we should have a common purpose. In this country in the past we have had a common purpose. I do not think it will be denied that a century ago, prior to confederation, there was a common purpose. Many in this house have spent years of their lives in an occupation which has certainly had a common purpose. I refer to war. We all know that in war there is a common purpose. When you have morale,

Vocational Training
with good officers and men, they are not girding at each other or working against each other. They believe in each other, and I see no reason in principle why we cannot have the same thing in civilian life.
There is just one other point I want to mention before I take my seat. I am not going to dwell on it because it is too big a problem to deal with in the last few minutes of a speech. One thing that would give us a common purpose would be if we really believed it was our task to go all out to raise the level of underdeveloped countries. That is not merely an emotional dream of long-haired enthusiasts. Eugene Black, head of the world bank, has stated in a most matter of fact way in a speech he made recently that we should be earnestly considering as part of our day to day obligations how much we can afford for these underdeveloped countries. Of course what he is pointing out is that it is not merely a case of doing the right thing or giving way to our better feelings, but also it is a case of taking steps to raise the level of world trade. It may be that in two, three or four years we may be saying to ourselves that in 1960 we could have done quite a lot about this, but we did not do it and consequently are suffering.
I think I have taken long enough. I am quite confident that the Minister of Labour will not be unmindful of this side of the picture. I have tried to say that I think it is possible to bring about what I have suggested provided we take the matter seriously. After all, some serious objective is necessary. I remember reading the other day of an American who had just returned from Moscow to Miami, and who found himself rather desolated in Miami because he said that when he left Moscow he left a city where people were working earnestly and seriously and believing in their work, however much we detested their aims, whereas when he got to Miami he found a different atmosphere. This serious, concentrated and devoted attitude toward life was entirely absent. It remains for us to choose which way we want to travel.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the general approval of this resolution there have been enough diverse approaches to suggest that we will only really grasp the scope and the direction when we see the legislation. For that reason I hope we will have a day or several days to look at the bill after it is introduced, because it is apparent that some people expect much more from the legislation than others.
We must have sympathy with the Minister of Labour and the government in this regard, because there are ten standards of education
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
which are going to be involved in this legislation and no one needs more sympathy than a federal legislator or executive who is trying to work out a common policy over the whole country on any educational matter. I feel that some members have perhaps cast their loop a little too wide with regard to what they expect from the legislation. Some of them seem to see it as a boost for technical schools, others as a boost for vocational training within the secondary schools, and others think it involves some kind of approach to apprenticeship training. Some see it, and this is the way I see it, as mainly an effort to do something about the unskilled people within the labour force who at the present time are almost unemployable.
I suppose it is out of order, Mr. Chairman, to refer to the proceedings of the other place, but there is a group there which is studying the whole manpower situation and which has already produced one paper that indicates the scope of the problem in attempting to define and set out what is involved in the working force. Right in that paper we have an indication that several hundred thousand people in this country are unemployable because of lack of skills. It is that very problem that I can see most strongly in my own region, and I wonder about the mechanics of this legislation and how it is going to be able to attack that problem.
Those of us who live in Ontario can be very proud of a number of institutions that our provincial government has fostered. I refer to Ryerson institute and the other technical institutes at Hamilton, Ottawa, Haileybury and Port Arthur, which are all doing very good work in catching people who are unable to go on within the university stream and yet can qualify as technicians. But I wonder if we really need to spend money in that particular field throughout the country if other parts of the country are on a par with Ontario. I wonder whether that is not too formal a kind of expenditure for the federal government to become involved in, and I am wondering whether it might not be better if in the spending of the money that is involved an attempt were made to hook up with local committees in various regions in an effort to bring about something that is fairly close to on the job training for people who are out of work.
Looking at the results from the application of schedule M in Ontario, I can only say they have been extremely disappointing. We have an advisory committee on vocational education at the lakehead working in cooperation with the unemployment insurance commission and the board of education. Despite repeated efforts they have only been able to get one course under way over a number

of years. That happened to be a very successful one, and one of the reasons for its success was that the instruction was given by practical men and was related directly to practical training for on the job work to fill an immediate need. In other words there was a great deal of flexibility about it. If you cannot retain flexibility under the plan now before us it seems to me that you have to fall back within the very large and swollen framework of the facilities provided by boards of education and the department of education in such institutions as vocational schools.
I think we need to keep this in mind, and I believe the teachers in the province of Ontario would agree wholeheartedly, that the vocational schools in Ontario have been a failure. I believe the scope and scale of that failure has never been underlined. When I say they have been a failure I mean they have been neither fish nor fowl. They have not provided a good general academic education, and they make very difficult the whole process of teaching. Perhaps this is not important, but it is very much to the point if you are trying to do something. They do not produce people who can go right out on the job and fit in very well.
One of the reasons for this, and this fits in with the remarks of the hon. gentleman who spoke just before me, is that you are trying to give them some kind of particular training at the same time you are trying to give them some kind of a general education. The mixture does not work very well. You can go to any board of education in Ontario that has a vocational school set-up and you will find that this is the most expensive kind of school, while the results that have been received from it are, in the main, extremely disappointing. When you talk to the employers of labour you will find it is only the very rare boy or girl who can really step out of a vocational school and make a contribution right away.

speechtext: What about the new institutes?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The hon. member asks about the new institutes, and they are a tremendous success. However, they are doing something quite different from what the vocational schools are doing. It is my considered opinion that we are wasting a great deal of money in Ontario on vocational training at the 14, 15 and 16 year age levels. We would be much better advised if we used these facilities to do the job done by the technical institutes to which the hon. member has referred. I think the record of the Ryerson institute has been good in filling an important need. We have had many students who have found, at grade XII or grade XIII, that they did not want to go on into university work and have turned
Vocational Training
to Ryerson and these other schools, and have had not only a practical success in finding good, well paying work, but a real stimulation in becoming topnotch technicians.
On the other hand, when I look at the record of our vocational schools and see what they turn out within the ordinary, secondary school framework, I can see nothing but disappointment. Many employers say they would much sooner have someone trained by a business college than someone who has been spoiled by a three-year commercial course at one of our vocational schools. I have gone to garage operators in Fort William and Port Arthur, where we have one of these vocational schools, and I have been told that there are very few good mechanics coming from these schools. Many of them tend to be spoiled by the fact that they get a superficial knowledge, and they have neither a good academic background nor a good mechanical training.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Would he say a word about the Ryerson institute, with which I am not familiar, and tell us to what extent it is exclusively technical?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The point here is that the Ryerson institute will only accept people who have completed or who are outside of the secondary school framework. It is not a secondary institution in any sense of the word. The whole idea is that they do give special courses of a technical kind and, in the main, Ryerson demands a qualification of at least grade XI and usually grade XII. It does wonderful remedial work on many people, too, in such fields as photography. People who have been to vocational schools and received some training there can go to Ryerson and receive a higher degree of training. Many of these vocational schools in terms of the money that has been pumped into them and in terms of the knowledge which they have pumped into the students, have been failures whereas these technical institutes, which are training people for higher, tougher, more concentrated standards, have proven to be a great success.
In Port Arthur, for example, the institute there is giving courses in two fields, mining and forestry. As a consequence we now have a number of technicians who are doing excellent jobs in both the fields of mining and pulp and paper. Many of these students, encouraged by their success as technicians, have returned to the universities to take degrees. We have one boy now who has his Ph.D. in geology, who dropped out of school at grade XII and then went on to take technical training and, encouraged by his success, returned to the university. In these cases the technical institutes have done a good job.

Vocational Training
I wonder whether this is really what we need, either the technical institute or support for our present vocational set-up. It seems to me that what we need is a much more pragmatic approach toward education of a practical kind which will do something for our unskilled people in the labour force. When we did get one course going at the lakehead, the number of people who wanted to take it was about four or five times the number who could. Amongst the unemployed I have repeatedly encountered the feeling that if there were only some way whereby they could receive training so they would at least be bulldozer operators, dragline operators or something like that, then their needs might be met. These courses should be conducted by experts grouped around some kind of regional centre, and it appears to me this type of course would be the most help.
One point that has become very obvious in the last few years has been underlined by this Senate report, and that is that the service industries are the real area of extension for our labour force, and that the primary goods, secondary goods and durable goods industries, as well as the basic industries, are either not growing at all or are in a stage of decline. This must raise the possibility of training men, in particular, in some aspects of the service industries, where the training does not have to be long but can be very practical, almost on the job. In the past women have been taking most of the jobs created by the expansion of the service industries. One of the things it seems to me we have to do is consider whether we cannot get more men into that part of our working force. Certainly, with the decline in the opportunities in the durable goods and basic industries, we have to take the time to get more money into the service industries. One of the reasons women have the advantage is that in the view of employers they tend to be more easily trained, more amenable to the kind of hours and the kind of working conditions there are in the service industries. It seems to me we might be able to do something in the way of a practical training program to get men into this particular field.
The last point I wanted to make was that all of us, no matter what our party, will have to have a tremendous amount of patience in regard to this particular program. Judging by the Ontario record, and the Ontario record in relation to the federal government, you are going to have recalcitrance, you are going to have delays. I personally am prepared to see this take a long, long time to get under way, even if we see that the terms under which it is to go ahead are good.
I hope the minister does not expect overnight success in getting this legislation going.

One thing that is probably going to be written into the legislation is some way of getting an expenditure in a hurry to help with the unemployment situation, to help get capital expenditures under way for the development of plant. This may be very well, and I hope that can be done. However, I do not think we can hope for complete implementation of this program for several years. I think where schedule M has failed, there is still some opportunity for success at very little expense in relation to what we may have under this program. I hope that is the way the government will try to make this mean something.
One of the things about which the hon. member for Peterborough and I were talking, as schoolteachers, was the change in attitude we have noticed in the last year and a half. I have been back as a supply teacher, and he has just come from the schoolroom.
In the last one and a half years we have noted a change in attitude on the part of students in the schools in which we happened to be and which are many hundreds of miles apart. The change could be summarized by saying that we now have motive of a much sharper kind back within the school framework. It is a pity that the motive must come from the unemployment situation and the tightening of the economy, but that is what we feel it to be.
I know the minister has made the point repeatedly that we must get the students to stay in school longer, that we must get them concerned about taking more intensive training, and that there must be a sharper motive on their part. To a degree the economic situation is beginning to supply this motive. I find that students are now much keener than they were just a few years ago.
In Port Arthur, in my opinion, the reason is that it is no longer possible for a student to quit school, go to the paper mill and get a good job at $1.75 or $2 an hour. Those opportunities are diminishing. The students are beginning to get an awareness that jobs are harder to come by and that education and training are quite important. This situation would seem to me to indicate that we are at the right stage or the ripe stage for a move in this regard. I hope this resolution will be a part of it. We are enthusiastic about the resolution though I expect that we shall be critical and suggestive about the legislation itself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
In rising to speak on this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to commend the government and the minister for this extremely practical and worth-while additional step to provide employment for all Canadians and train the

technicians that are needed in this country-in this day and age. Like other hon. members who have already spoken, including the hon. member who has just done so, have a personal interest in this measure because my profession is and always has been that of teaching in the specific branch of vocational education.
Education itself, as everyone knows, is a provincial responsibility, so decreed under the British North America Act. This provision was evidently necessary at confederation because of geography, race and religion, but it seems to me that it is not a valid reason today. A few years ago, in the promotion for education week across the dominion, the slogan was "Education is everybody's business". I thoroughly agree with that sentiment.
It is only in the last half century or so that there has been any vocational training in the schools. The hon. member who immediately preceded me took a rather pessimistic view of vocational training. I cannot agree with him completely, although in some cases it does not seem to have fulfilled the objectives contemplated. However, I believe this action which is being taken by the federal government to further vocational and technical training will commend itself to all Canadians.
It is true that there are ten standards of education in Canada. However, after the last war, when-" approximately one million service men and women left the forces, there were several hundred thousand of them who wanted training in universities, vocational schools and business colleges as well as other on the job training of various kinds. At that particular time it was not found impossible to use all the facilities of every department of education in Canada in order to train those men and women. I see no reason why the same accommodation cannot be brought about today in order to make this particular program and the extension of this act a complete success. I shall discuss that matter a little further in these brief remarks.
The greatest proportion of those who are unemployed in this country today, as we all know only too well, are those who have little education and little or no specific skill. There is a fine pamphlet put out by the Department of Labour. It is entitled "Are you thinking of leaving school?" I suppose all hon. members have copies of this pamphlet. So much material comes to our desks that quite often we do not get the opportunity to read it all, however, I would commend this pamphlet to every hon. member. It contains some extremely pertinent facts in connection with the training of our youth and their lack of education.
Vocational Training
According to this pamphlet, a survey shows that 63.5 per cent of those who are unemployed today in Canada or of those who are seeking work today-perhaps that is a better way of expressing the matter-have had only a grade VIII education or less. All those people can offer an employer is just unskilled labour. We used to say-it is not very humorous, and I do not mean it to be humorous- that all they can offer is a strong back and a weak mind. Perhaps the thought would be better expressed by saying that all they can offer is a strong back and an untrained mind.
There are also those who do not wish to work. That is a sad commentary on our modern civilization and this welfare state into which we have been ushered in the last 25 years. I know of one community- and I suppose this statement could apply to practically every town and city in Can-ada-in which there is a group of young men in their late teens or early twenties who are referred to as the leather jacket brigade. There happens to be about 35 or 40 persons in this group. When they are referred to a job they will stay on it only until somebody gives them an order. Then they will walk out, but before they walk out they want to know when they are going to be paid.
Perhaps nothing very much can be done about those young people; I do not know. I doubt that this particular group is trainable. However, there are a great many young men and young women who, through force of circumstances and perhaps through lack of wisdom on their part when they were young-we all go through this stage but fortunately some of us outgrow it eventually- have no training whatsoever, and they are the ones who are worthy of help. This measure will assist them.
What is the reason there are so many unemployed in this country today? There are more persons working now than ever before in the history of Canada. However, there are more people coming into our labour force every year than the economy is able to absorb. The answer, I believe, is to be found partly but not completely in automation. The other day I read a definition of automation. It was a rather heavy one; this is it: Automation is a term which we loosely apply and is of comparatively recent origin, which has gained wide currency to describe a specific aspect of mechanization applied to operations formerly performed by manual labour.
We have heard much said about automation. Machinery has been gradually taking over many jobs, doing them more efficiently and making life more pleasant for all of us. The champions of automation point out that

Vocational Training
more jobs are created in the process than are done away with. This statement is probably true. However, those new jobs are for the most part skilled jobs. Firms which introduce new machinery usually make every effort to retrain the unskilled employees for the new jobs. This training or retraining is extremely difficult and in some cases impossible if those employees do not have the fundamental knowledge or the fundamental, basic education on which such training can be based. The employees who cannot be retrained are laid off. If they find other unskilled jobs, the chances are that they will soon be laid off again. Each new invention since the invention of the wheel-perhaps the greatest invention in the history of mankind-has meant change and temporary distress. Such has been the situation through the centuries. We are experiencing today a temporary dislocation of our work force.
I should like to relate a personal experience in connection with retraining having regard to this subject about which we are talking today and actually under this act which is being amended. In 1954, in the little cotton milling town of Marysville, close to Fredericton where I make my home, the mill which had been in operation for 75 years making good textiles was forced to close. It was a great blow to the community because people there, from the time they had started their working days-some of them extremely young, perhaps too young-had worked nowhere else but in this textile mill.
The action of the government at that particular time I felt was most commendable. The then federal minister of labour, who was the representative of that constituency in the House of Commons, got together with the very able minister of labour in the province of New Brunswick, who served in that government under the present distinguished Minister of Forestry, and their cooperation was a fine thing to see. I wish all governments and individuals were able to co-operate as they did at that time. They took a large proportion of these people and put them into training courses. I was personally interested, because I was directly concerned with helping to train between 35 and 40 of them in the field of commercial education.
What were the results? People who one day seemed to have no hope went back to school and, for the most part, did well. It is true that a few of them did not, not because they were too old or anything of that kind but they just could not make the grade. On the other hand, some of them did very well indeed. The great bulk of those who were

dealt with were satisfactorily retrained and went out to take their places in industry, and in business offices.
I should like to quote a paragraph or so from Industry, which is a publication of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association:
A high proportion of those out of a job for any length of time stay jobless either because they are unskilled or because demand for their particular skill is not what it was.
At the same time, employers, newspaper advertisements and national employment service bulletins daily emphasize the fact that there are other skills which are-and have been for some considerable time-very much in demand. Clearly, what is needed is a much more ambitious, energetic and nationwide program of job training and retraining than anything we have yet attempted in Canada.
Belgium, as the Labour Gazette recently pointed out, is one country which has shown what can be done. She has retrained more than 25,000 unemployed persons over the past 15 years and over the same period has developed her retraining program to the point where it is today one of the most advanced in the free world.
Training centres are located in various parts of the country. These operate within the framework of a highly flexible training system that adapts the kinds of trades taught to the nation's economic needs as forecast by a manpower studies unit. Length of an average course is five to eight months, but this is shortened where possible.
A Belgian who successfully completes his course is considered to be semi-qualified; a few more months of practical experience usually is enough to make him fully skilled. Although most trainees are in their twenties or thirties, some are older, the retraining program being quite separate from the regular vocational training program for school leavers.
There would seem to be no reason why Canada could not profit from Belgian experience and, indeed, from that of other industrial countries which have gone further along these lines than we have.
We are certainly in a position to know which industrial and commercial skills are going to be needed most in the years immediately ahead.
I think that is a very fine article. Our able and progressive government is taking a long stride in the right direction in bringing forward this measure. Some hon. members of this house have visited the communist countries, Russia and China, in the last year or two. We cannot disregard the fact that Russia and China are making terrific strides in technical training. Unfortunately they are at the same time neglecting what we consider to be the finer aspects of education. However, I do not think that will happen in this country of ours. We know that in the next decade our universities will have hundreds of thousands more students than they have at the present time, and today they are filled almost to capacity. While we may disagree with the militant system of communism-and we all do in this house-let us not bury our heads in the sand so that we cannot see the tremendous strides they are making technologically.

The other day I read a fine article in the editorial page of the Ottawa Journal, and I should like to quote a short portion of it. For me the editorial page of any newspaper contains much that is well worth reading as, I am sure, most hon. members will agree. This particular article said in part:
Provincial and municipal authorities can help prevent the waste of human resources if they plan at once to supplement the dominion program of assistance to vocational training.
Without their co-operation, the offer of the federal government to pay 75 per cent of the cost of approved technical schools or training institutions will achieve little, although buildings should go up quickly.
At the various levels of government it is known that buildings are only a start. The important part of the program is the bringing to them of students who want to be trained, and can be trained, for useful work in which they can have pride and adequate reward for their skill.
The writer points out that the important part of the program for new schools is the student. It seems to me that there is another factor which is most important. To me the most important factor in any school is the man or woman who stands at the head of the classroom. I think that for far too many decades, or even centuries, the teachers have been the forgotten persons in the school system. They were underpaid and overworked. It is only in the last few years that teachers have been adequately paid in this country, though the teachers play the most important part of all. We must not forget that the greatest lesson ever taught in the history of mankind was taught on the side of a hill and it was called the Sermon on the Mount. It was not necessary to have a million dollar school building in order to teach that lesson.
It would be naive to think that a multitude of students waits to bang on the doors for admission when the new training schools are finished. The idea of training, or retraining, has to be sold. Encouragement and explanation may not suffice; to ensure that the training program yields the results it should, there may have to be more positive action. Thousands of young men, it has been estimated, left high school in the last year and have been unable to find regular employment. Most of them would benefit from training for useful occupations, but such is the contrariness of youth that unless there is positive direction many will continue to drift.
There is a source of teachers which I should like to mention briefly. This would require a great deal of co-operation among the various departments of government. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the armed forces of this country have fine technical and training schools. I have had some experience in connection with the army, and perhaps that is why I think of the Royal
Vocational Training
Canadian Engineers, the Royal Canadian Electrical and Mechanical Engineers and the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals, for example. If this program is to be put over I suggest to the minister that he explore the possibility of obtaining on loan highly skilled and highly trained technical instructors from the army.
In conclusion, entering into all these considerations is the human factor. Next to a man's family his job is the most important thing in the world to him, his chance and his right to earn a decent living. I am sure other hon. members of this house are as distressed as I am when they talk to a decent man with a family who, through no fault of his own, cannot get employment; or when they talk to a young man who, because of his lack of training cannot get a job, whether it is his fault or somebody else's fault. It is always distressing, and these people are very close to us; whether or not we know them personally we all sympathize deeply. If this measure will do anything to help such people it is one of the most worth-while measures this house could pass during the present session, and I would ask every hon. member to give it his full and unqualified support.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on this resolution concerning vocational and technical training. This is a subject in which I am exceedingly interested, and I should like to take a few minutes to talk about it here at the present time.
We have wonderful winter works program committees in Chilliwack and Mission city in my constituency, and these committees more or less put the punch into the winter works program.
The dominion and provincial governments have continuously stressed the importance of the workers acquiring the skills necessary to keep pace with modern industry. A survey of the 5,177 pupils attending junior and senior high school in Chilliwack, Abbotsford, Mission, Sardis, Yarrow, Fraser Canyon and Agassiz districts indicates that 654 of these dropped out last year, and of this number approximately 165 would have been interested in vocational training had it been available to them.
According to the latest figures from the British Columbia department of education, approximately 64 per cent of all students entering high school do not graduate. This would indicate to me, and I am sure to other hon. members, that many students find academic training either too difficult or of no practical use to them. Rather than have these students drop out to become merely manual labourers or unemployed, it would seem good business to provide for suitable

Vocational Training
training more closely tied to the vocational needs of the student and the country's economy. After early counselling in grade VIII or IX, if it is found that they have the aptitude and are anxious to learn a trade the students should be offered suitable vocational training.
The national employment service in Chilliwack is continually contacted by young people who have been out of school several years, by handicapped workers and by older married workers who possess outmoded skills, seeking additional vocational training. Many of these would have been suitable for training but have had to wait so long to be accepted into a school that they drifted into low paying, unskilled and unsuitable employment. Because of the extremely large number of applications received by the Vancouver vocational institute it is expected that an applicant would have to wait approximately a year to receive the training he desired. At latest report the Nanaimo vocational training school on Vancouver island is also operating at capacity, and an applicant has often had to wait a year to receive training there. Of the applicants who were not able to receive training at Vancouver or Nanaimo, a large number who reside at the coast, in the interior and in various parts of British Columbia would be agreeable to taking their training in the Fraser valley should a vocational school be established there.
I think it is a sound principle that any special training, whether or not it is immediately useful, is an asset to the individual and to the community. An education of any kind is a handy thing to carry around. It might even be more important to some students to know how to repair a car than to be able to keep a set of books. Without adequate vocational schools situated in strategic positions throughout the country it is impossible for students to get this training.
A resolution passed last year by the Chilliwack winter works committee reads as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that the dominion and provincial governments allocate moneys for the construction of a vocational training school, at Chilliwack or somewhere in the upper Fraser valley on a winter works program project, to provide training in such generally useful subjects as auto and diesel mechanics, auto body, commerce-
-and believe it or not the committee even included-
-beauty culture and barbering.
The establishment of such a vocational training school would fill a great need in the Fraser valley. It could be patterned along the lines of the school in Nanaimo. I know several young men who attended school in

Nanaimo and who are now happily employed as mechanics. I know of two students in particular who were unsuccessful in high school and who are now extremely successful in mechanical work. The father of one of the boys at one time wondered what he was going to do with his son, but now this lad is happily employed.
I received several letters after coming to Ottawa in relation to the resolution to which I have made reference. The letters came from such groups as the Ryder lake P.T.A., the Canadian Order of Foresters and the Ryder lake branch of the British Columbia women's institutes. All expressed their support for the resolution. I even received from the Chilliwack and district ministerial association a resolution which said, in part, that the different levels of government be asked to consider-
-the establishing of an educational program for those young men who are capable of using it. Social workers remind us that the great majority of these young people want work, but because of their lack of training, are usually the first casualties of a recession.
Late last summer a vocational school opened in Burnaby. This school was constructed by the province of British Columbia under the federal-provincial vocational and technical training agreement. We had approved a federal contribution of $1,101,276.71 toward the capital cost of this project. It is difficult to say how much has been contributed to the operation of this particular school, because our allotment to the provinces for operation is an allotment to programs rather than schools, and some of the programs in British Columbia, such as that for the training of unemployed persons, are carried out in other schools such as Nanaimo and the Vancouver vocational institute, as well as at Burnaby. However, under the agreement mentioned about the sum of $227,800 was allotted to British Columbia in 1959-60 for the operation of vocational training programs.
Under the federal-provincial special vocational training projects agreement the sum of $167,869.31 was paid for the operation of vocational programs including training of unemployed persons, foremen and supervisors and workers in primary industries. Under the federal-provincial apprenticeship agreement the sum of $341,924.79 was paid to British Columbia in 1959-60 for the training of industrial apprentices.
More vocational and technical training of youth is required with the advance of technology in industry. Indeed, the retraining of many workers is almost as important if production is to be increased. Transferring from one job to another is also important. With the anticipated jump in export trade

due to the extension of new credit to exporters it is important that the production of many articles be improved.
Some say we do not want too many vocational schools. I have no fear of this, as the demand for skilled workers is sure to increase. I feel that the idea of suitable grants for research work from the standpoint of vocational and technical education is deserving of our encouragement.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to this resolution I conducted a small investigation with the Department of Labour as to the number of unplaced applicants as of October 31. I believe these figures not only indicate the need of this measure proposed by the Minister of Labour but illustrate the vital necessity of it.
For instance, on October 31 unplaced applicants in the professional and managerial class represented 12 per cent of the vacancies but only 2 per cent of the applications. As of the same date 28 per cent of the total number of personnel registered for employment with the national employment service were totally unskilled. This group would not include even the semi-skilled jobs such as waitress and other jobs of that nature. The figure represents those who had no training whatsoever in any type of job.
With respect to the vacancies, there were 28 per cent applying for them but only 15 per cent of the vacancies were for unskilled labour. At the end of September there were 4,448 vacancies which could not be filled from local offices and had to be put into clearance; that is, they had to be put into a system whereby the request for help was funnelled through all offices of the national employment service. At that time the requests were for 150 engineers, 65 draftsmen, 207 nurses, 17 land surveyors, 5 credit checkers and 80 machinists. These were the types of jobs that were put into clearance because they could not be filled from local offices. It is granted that because of variations in economic activities in different parts of the country we may have a shortage of machinists in one office and a surplus in another, and that is why they have the clearance arrangement, so that those shortages can be made known to offices where there is a likelihood that they can fill the requirements.
I was also interested in an article entitled "The Growing Shortage of Technicians" by Paul Nowack, which appeared in Saturday Night of September 3, 1960. The article starts off in the following way;
The demand for highly trained personnel has never been greater in the nation's history. The classified advertising pages in newspapers from coast to coast bear witness to it. But leaders in industry who are worried about the current shortage of trained technical personnel, are even more 90205-6-35
Vocational Training
concerned about the future. All agree that many more specialists are essential if our increasingly automated, industrialized society is to vie successfully with fierce world competition.
The same article later on quotes Thomas Medland, executive director of the association of professional engineers of Ontario, who stated that the ratio of three technicians to one engineer is not high enough for Canada. The article continues:
He claims that the proper ratio is five to one. Right now it stands at less than one and a half to one. Medland asserts this low ratio is the real cause of the so-called shortage of engineers.
The point that is being made, of course, is something that is rather difficult to grasp immediately, that at a time of very high unemployment-because, according to the dominion bureau of statistics figures, on October 15 there were 368,000 persons in Canada seeking work-we have a shortage of trained personnel. Part of the answer over the years has been immigration, the bringing into Canada of skilled people, and part of the answer has been again on the job experience; but neither of these is the real answer to the problem. The real answer is to gauge our requirements for technically trained people and provide the facilities to teach and train previously unskilled people to handle those technical jobs.
We are coming to a period, in fact we have already entered into it, when we require more training in schools. We require a longer schooling period. We require an extended teacher training program. We require all these things because of the growing complexity of industry and the increasing technical requirements of industry. If we are to increase our export trade, if we are to have a continuing level of prosperity in this country, then we must do it by better use of materials, machinery and men.
This resolution deals with the last of these three items, the better utilization of men and women through training to take the jobs which are in industry and which will be created by industry as our industrial capacity increases. This adequate supply of trained technical help will be of immeasurable benefit in the expansion of our industrial activity. In this way it will generally increase employment throughout, whether that employment is in the service industries, in the professional fields, business, insurance, finance or whatever it may be; the increasing industrial base which we will achieve, partly through resolutions and measures such as this and partly through other measures which have been brought in and will be brought before the house. This is one of the best

Vocational Training
ways to attack the major underlying problem we have in Canada today, namely unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, the bill forecast by the resolution introduced by the Minister of Labour is of great interest to all parts of Canada. It will, I am sure, be a great help toward our country's continued national development. I want to join with the other speakers in offering congratulations to the minister on this far-sighted move which, as he stated, is designed to undergird the government's program for increasing employment and fostering national development.
The proposed bill is aimed at stimulating and encouraging technical and vocational training by broadening the scope of this training. The changing pattern of manpower requirements emphasizes the need for such action, because anyone who has made any study of the present unemployment situation realizes that, in the midst of this unemployment, there is a big demand for skilled and technical workmen.
The minister pointed out that Canada has never trained enough manpower to meet the needs of Canadian industry. I was surprised at his statement that a survey of five skilled occupations showed that only 35 per cent of the workers in those occupations had been trained in Canada. We should be able to train a much higher proportion of our skilled workers. The program of training embodied in this resolution is intended to accomplish this.
The minister indicated that further research will be carried on to show how labour demands are changing, and the resulting recommendations should be given all the publicity possible, especially in labour circles. In this regard, I think labour leaders would assist by putting greater emphasis on the growing need for more education and for greater training. This could also be done through the Canadian vocational training advisory council, which consists of representatives of employers, labour and the provincial governments. The minister pointed out that the bill he will bring in is patterned along the line of recommendations from this advisory council.
Mr. Chairman, other speakers have referred to an editorial reprinted in Canadian Weekly Features. I should like to refer to it briefly because I think it throws light on the training program we are now considering. It starts off by saying:
There are several reasons why unemployment remains stubbornly and uncomfortably high. But, without a doubt, a high proportion of those out of a job for any length of time stay jobless either because they are unskilled or because demand for their particular skill is not what it was.

The editorial goes on to say:
At the same time, employers, newspaper advertisements and national employment service bulletins daily emphasize the fact that there are other skills which are and have been for some considerable time very much in demand. Clearly, what is needed is a much more ambitious, energetic and nation-wide program of job training and retraining than anything we have yet attempted in Canada.
I submit that the program forecast by the Minister of Labour is just such a training program.
Other speakers have already mentioned what Belgium has done with regard to training and retraining. As was pointed out, that country has retrained more than 25,000 unemployed persons over the past 15 years and over the same period has developed its retraining program to a point where it is today one of the most advanced in the free world. With regard to what Belgium has done, the editorial goes on to say:
There would seem to be no reason why Canada could not profit from Belgian experience and, indeed, from that of other industrial countries which have gone further along these lines than we have.
The editorial states that Belgium has been carrying on this training for 15 years or more. I mention this to draw attention to the lack of action on this problem by the previous government. While Belgium and other countries for years were moving very effectively to increase the skills of their workers in order to fit them for the changing pattern of available employment, the previous federal government apparently was not. As a result we have many people unemployed at a time when there is a demand for skilled workers. I think this situation constitutes an indictment of the previous government for its lack of foresight and lack of action in past years.

I will refer to that right now. My home city of Moose Jaw will be particularly interested in the minister's proposals. The resolution refers to contributions or grants by the federal government toward the cost of capital expenditures on facilities for vocational and technical training. Through such federal financial help, and I bring this to the attention of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, amounting to more than $2,186,000 up to the end of this fiscal year, a fine technical institute has been constructed and is now operating in Moose Jaw for vocational and technical training. In this regard, Mr. Chairman, there has been some mention by previous speakers that vocational and technical training institutes should be established at many points in the various provinces. Saskatchewan Is going through a period of social and economic change. At the end of the war a little over 20 per cent of our total production was non-agricultural... At a meeting of the vocational training advisory council in Ottawa this year it was emphasized that the provinces are expanding the training of unemployed workers. Members of the council agreed that although increased training of workers without jobs was not the complete answer to the problem of unemployment such training could go a long way toward alleviating the situation. It was brought to the attention of the advisory council that while registrations of those seeking jobs increased at national employment offices, at the same time there were numbers of unfilled jobs because those seeking work did not have the skills required for the jobs that were open.
One speaker told the meeting that there was a growing recognition of the importance and the necessity of training and general education as a basic requirement in improving Canada's long term employment outlook. In so far as this training of unemployed workers is concerned, I think it is a fine move on the part of the government to allow those wishing to attend classes to do so while they are drawing unemployment insurance. I believe, Mr. Chairman, there should be more publicity given to this training of the unemployed while they are drawing their unemployment insurance, with the federal government paying 75 per cent of the cost, as I pointed out before. Again, I compliment the Minister of Labour for this action he has taken, and I am very happy to. support the resolution.
