speechtext:
I think one should add to the words of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that this afternoon we have heard from a great number of the supporters of the government. They, of course, are free to take part in the debate. It is the government supporters, in the main, rather than the members of the opposition who are making it impossible for the request of the Minister of Labour to be granted. In other word's, the members of the Conservative party have told the Minister of Labour they do not agree with his suggestion to pass the resolution, and they are going to talk about it.
Last night, when the house leader was reporting the business of the house, I noticed he suggested that we might take both readings of the bill today. I think this is doing things backwards. If there is a stage of the debate that should be shortened, it should be this stage and then we should have at least overnight to look at the bill rather than adopt the procedure that apparently the government wants us to adopt, namely a dragged out debate on the resolution, with exceedingly meagre information before the committee, and then wrap up the bill in a very short time with members obviously not having a chance to study the bill. The position of this group has already been placed on the record by a number of our members such as the hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Peterborough, the hon. member for Port Arthur, so my remarks will not be extensive at this stage.
However, I do want to point out what the committee is being asked to do. We are being asked to pass this resolution with almost no information having been given to the committee by the minister as to the contents of the bill. As I see it, we should have been told whether or not a survey is going to be undertaken to ascertain the requirements in Canada for the training of personnel under this type of legislation. The minister has been
[Mr. Pascoe.l
able to give us statistics to show that a large number of those that are unemployed are unskilled, but we have no information as to the number of skilled persons who are required in the various categories throughout the country. I ask the minister if that information is available to him. Has the gov-ment any idea whatever of the number of trained persons in the various categories required by the labour market in our country at this time?
Is this part of a co-ordinated policy to make reasonably certain that the graduates of vocational training schools will have jobs available or is this just another case of a hit and miss, patchwork effort by the government which has very little to do with a well thought out program to meet the need for a greater number of skilled workers in this country and to provide graduates of vocational training schools with jobs? I would ask the minister, too, whether under this legislation there has been any thought given to the making of payments to dependents of persons who are being trained. It is obvious that if unemployed persons must maintain families there must be some provision for the maintenance of their dependents during the time the unemployed person is being trained.
I take it from the resolution, but I cannot take it from the minister's speech because it is not there, that the government, under the legislation that will follow, is prepared to take some initiative to make certain that technical and vocational training is provided because there is one section in the resolution which would empower the minister to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons. I would ask the minister to tell the committee what is the particular provision in this bill which will make this possible. Undoubtedly, we need technical training for Canadians at this time because of widespread unemployment. I think an improvement in the educational facilities in the vocational field is necessary in Canada, even if we had a full employment economy. As automation is accelerated there will be a greater and greater need for moneys from the federal government and from governments at all levels to provide additional facilities in the field of adult education, in the field of vocational training and others.
I would ask the minister, before he requests the committee to pass this resolution, to tell the committee the main features of the bill. The hon. member for Essex East says, let us see the bill. I am not satisfied, myself, with the minister's statement which is so empty of content. I think the Minister of Labour should have been as frank with the

committee as were his colleagues during this session in introducing other legislation. The Minister of Public Works, in introducing the resolution which preceded the amendments to the National Housing Act, was frank with the committee. He told us the main features that would be contained in the bill. We were not asked to discuss a resolution without any information, because we were given the principal features of the bill. I suggest that this practice should have been followed by the Minister of Labour in asking the house to discuss and to support this resolution.
The Minister of Finance was frank with the house when he presented a resolution which preceded the bill to provide certain loan facilities to small businessmen in this country. The Minister of Finance outlined the main principles of the bill. The house was able to deal with that resolution in an informed way because we knew the main features contained in the bill. This time we are asked to pass the resolution and then we are asked to pass the bill on the same day without having been given any real information by the Minister of Labour as to the main features of the bill.
I think this procedure is an insult to the committee. I think it is a rather contemptuous procedure to ask parliament and the members of the house to discuss intelligently and to vote in an intelligent manner when the Minister of Labour has refused to disclose in his statement the main features of the bill that is to follow the resolution.
In former days, when the Conservative party sat on the opposition side of the house, they raised their voices strongly in asking the government at the time of a resolution to disclose the principal features that would be in the bill. I think this procedure is making a mockery of this stage of the debate when the Minister of Labour gives us almost no information and then we have an endless stream of Conservative members standing up to congratulate the minister and saying what a wonderful thing he is doing. He has not told us just what he is going to do but they are so happy about it that they are congratulating him. They are spending the time of the House of Commons in discussing a question about which the Minister of Labour has given us almost no information.
I have carefully gone over the statement initially made by the minister. I have looked for him to spell out some of the main points outlined in the resolution that we are asked to pass. This is something he has failed to do. This procedure, I feel, is not giving parliament its right to discuss in an informed manner the resolution which the government would like to see passed. We are all in favour
Vocational Training
of an extension of vocational training facilities. However, instead of a government short term filibuster on its own resolution, it would be much better and in keeping with the practices of our House of Commons for the minister to have given the committee the same kind of general outline of the main features of the bill to follow this resolution as was given by the Minister of Finance in announcing legislation having to do with small business and as was given by the Minister of Public Works at the resolution stage preceding the bill to amend the National Housing Act.
I ask the Minister of Labour to tell the members of the committee the main features of this resolution and to cease trying to keep us in the dark and asking us to pass a resolution about which he has given us little information.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting my bill at this time I realize this may be a controversial measure, but as I have gone about the country I have found there are a great many people who believe that something should be done at this time by way of authorizing a distinctive national flag. I

have some notes here and 1 should like to stick to them fairly closely since this may be a controversial matter.
In proposing the second reading of Bill No. C-8 at this time I do so with all sincerity and respect for the two flags which Canada now uses-the union jack and the red ensign-and I appreciate the heritage of pride and devotion for those flags which our armed forces and our pioneer Canadians have left for us by having used them during days of both victory and misfortune. Had I been in this house 20 years ago, it is doubtful whether I would have sponsored a bill of this kind, although as far back as the first world war I often felt that Canada some day should have a distinctive Canadian flag.
In my opinion that day has now arrived, and with our population now soaring to 18 million people of all creeds and races, and bearing in mind the outstanding part Canada is playing in world affairs, we need a distinctive Canadian flag that leaves no doubt as to our identity among nations.
This bill advances no opinions as to what the flag should be like or what group of people or what committee should design it. If we agree in principle that Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag then I am sure that on another occasion this house could determine what procedure could be taken by way of setting up a special committee or taking any other action to determine the design and colour of the flag itself. In recent years I have observed many acts of indiscretion and neglect in the use of our flag, or flags, by both Canadian and other people, and I am sure the majority of Canadian people would welcome action by this government to designate a distinctive Canadian flag, giving some direction of when and where it should be used.
In my own home city of St. Catharines I find that the city council continue to fly the union jack at the city hall whereas the Lincoln county council flies the red ensign on the county building which stands in the city square next to St. Catharines' city hall. This is most confusing, especially to new Canadians and children.
On the Welland ship canal which passes through my riding of Lincoln the same condition of uncertainty about our flag prevails. Foreign shipmasters, who are expected to fly a Canadian flag on their ships while passing through Canadian inland waters are often confused and sometimes do not fly either the union jack or the red ensign. In fact, I see some of them flying the United States flag where the Canadian flag should be.
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that the appreciation of our flag or flags, and what

they stand for is deteriorating in the minds of some Canadian people. Too often we see the union jack and the red ensign tacked up to trees and fence posts at auction sales and the opening of new gasoline stations, and left to become tattered and weather beaten.
I think all this lack of courtesy, respect and love for our flags could be and should be corrected as soon as possible by the dedication of a distinctive Canadian flag. Personally, I would not object to adopting the red ensign which was originally a British naval flag. Perhaps, with some slight modifications, this flag could be made to be the unanimous choice of the Canadian people.
The council of the corporation of the city of St. Catharines, which is located in my riding, realizing the need for a distinctive Canadian flag, passed the following resolution asking the Prime Minister and his government to enact legislation to establish a distinctive Canadian flag:
Moved by Alderman Beattie:
Seconded by Alderman Chown:
Whereas this council is aware that, on the fifth day of September 1945, the federal government by its order in council, Number P.C. 5888, declared it appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign within and without Canada, wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag;
And whereas it is unanimously conceded that Canada, by its active participation in important world affairs and as part of the British commonwealth, has served with distinction, not only in defence of Canada alone or in particular, but also served valiantly in defence of the British empire;
And whereas the population of Canada now numbers approximately eighteen million persons as citizens of Canada;
And whereas Canada is the only nation and member of the British commonwealth of nations and in fact, the only nation in the world that has no national flag of its own;
Now therefore be it resolved that the federal government and the Right Honourable the Prime Minister of Canada be and they are hereby required to amend order in council P.C. 5888 or to pass a new order in council to provide forthwith for the establishment of a distinctive Canadian flag;
And further that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Right Honourable John Diefenbaker, and to Mr. John Smith, member of parliament for Lincoln county, and to all members of the federal cabinet, urging their vigorous support and that copies be sent to all Ontario county councils and to all municipal councils of every city and town in Ontario, requesting them to pass a similar resolution and submit the same to their respective local member of parliament as well as to Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, urging upon them the necessity of this important and vital subject.
Copies of that resolution were sent out to all municipal councils in the province of Ontario, with the result that I have on loan from the city of St. Catharines a file which contains replies from 98 of those municipalities. Fifty three of those municipalities are in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag,
Flags of Canada
17 are undecided, and 28 feel that it is entirely a matter for the government at Ottawa to deal with. They declined to take any action although some of those 28 indicated they would have endorsed the St. Catharines resolution if it had asked that the red ensign be dedicated as a distinctive Canadian flag. Should the Canadian government decide to have a distinctive Canadian flag, I am sure the union jack will always be flown in Canada with perhaps more reverence as the British flag, the empire flag, than it is now. At the present time it is sometimes used as just another flag. I think I have submitted enough evidence to show there is a growing feeling among Canadians that Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag so that this difference of opinion on which flag to fly and when to fly it may be clarified.
I hope that if not sufficient time is available to discuss this bill at this time the government will make more time available in the near future or bring in a government bill similar to Canada's bill of rights 1960.
I have been asked on several occasions by tourists why there is no Canadian flag flying on the Peace Tower or any part of the centre block on week ends or when parliament is not in session. I understand it is against certain regulations to fly a flag from the Peace Tower of the House of Commons unless the members of parliament are in the house at work or sitting in the house. If this is so, surely somewhere on parliament hill there could be a flag pole worthy of the Canadian capital where our flag could be raised in the morning and lowered at sundown with pride and dignity. I am a great believer in flag-raising ceremonies at schools, universities and other places of learning. I believe it is necessary that our young people and our new Canadian citizens should, as a foundation for their citizenship, be taught to respect and love a distinctive Canadian flag.
I do not think it proper that they have to make their own choice between the union jack, the red ensign, or a provincial flag while we who should know better are still divided on whether we should continue to use or not to use the red ensign, which was a British naval flag the British Admiralty permitted Canada to use in 1892 and which by order in council in 1945 the Canadian cabinet declared it appropriate to use on certain occasions.
That is the extent of my submission on behalf of a distinctive Canadian flag. I feel that hon. members who favour it will speak to it and those who are opposed to it will do likewise. It seems to me that for the past 68 years, ever since the British Admiralty gave us permission to use the red ensign, the people of Canada have been divided on the question of a distinctive flag. Our neighbours

Flags of Canada
across the border in the United States have a far better conception of a national flag than we have. I go over there occasionally and am always impressed by their flag-raising ceremonies. If we could decide on a distinctive flag I do not think it would be too long before all Canadians would adopt it, love it and respect it.
At this time there comes to my mind occasions when flags were raised under very trying circumstances. I recall the United States troops at the Pacific island of Okinawa when a group of United States soldiers seized the flag of that country, rushed to the top of a hill and raised it. If they did not have a distinctive flag what would they have done?
I also recall a moving incident in the first war in the battle of Pozieres ridge. An Australian soldier crept to the top of the ridge, stuck his rifle in the ground, hung his helmet from it, hung from the top a small flag he carried in his hip pocket, and then died. The memory of that action by that Australian soldier still lingers with us. Every year at armistice we all think of it as a symbol of sacrifice.
I could speak at length on this bill but I should like to conclude these remarks at this time because I know that time is limited.

Then we shall see if he shares Mr. Smallwood's way of thinking or not.
Mr. Speaker, there have been two incidents at the international level because we had no distinctive Canadian flag. In 1944, the Argentina opposed our joining the PanAmerican union, because we had no distinctive flag. There had been some confusion with another country. Moreover, from a practical point of view, the lack of a distinctive flag caused some difficulties for our country. We may remember the Egyptian attitude, when those people refused to welcome troops flying the British flag when the Canadians arrived in the Middle East.
But it was mostly in our national pride that we have had to suffer from a state of affairs for which there is no excuse in the case of an international power such as Canada is at the present time.
As for the red ensign, may I add, Mr. Speaker, that it was unquestionably to an order of the Admiralty, dating back to February 2, 1892 that prime minister Mackenzie King was referring on June 9, 1943, when he stated in reply to a question of an hon. member, Mr. Wilfrid Lacroix, that it was a mistake to contend that Canada had no flag.

Of course, our ships are now allowed to fly the British naval flag bearing the arms of Canada, especially since 1936 when paragraph 1 of section 89 of the Canada Shipping Act was amended to confirm-one wonders why -the Admiralty's order.
May that flag be used on land? Custom forbids it. "The red ensign, says Stewart Wallace, is essentially a naval flag, that may not be flown on land." He goes on to say that the flag may not, therefore, constitute Canada's national flag.
Nevertheless, by virtue of an order of the privy council under date of January 26, 1924, permission was granted to fly the naval blue ensign (the distinctive flag of Canadian coast guard vessels, as authorized by the admiralty in 1868) on Canada House in London and to use the red ensign, with the Canadian coat of arms of course, on all dominion buildings or buildings occupied by Canadian representatives outside Canada.
Therefore, that essentially naval flag has become the distinctive standard on our consulates, commissioner's offices, legations and embassies abroad.
Was the British Admiralty consulted in that instance? I doubt it very much. In any case the Admiralty is much less concerned with its prerogatives than it used to be concerning those emancipated children which the dominions now constitute within the British family of nations.
If a commonwealth nation wishes to use a naval flag on land, authorities in the mother country will only smile as they might if an Iroquois or a Huron chose to saunter down Regent street in a feather headdress and moccasins.
Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity, at the beginning of this session, to introduce a bill concerning a distinctive national flag and a distinctive national anthem.
Soon Canada will celebrate the centennial of confederation. Already, in many parts of the country plans are under way to celebrate the one hundredth anniversary of Canadian nationhood adequately and logically.
Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that the best way to pay tribute to our forebearers is to recognize nationally that Canada is autonomous and free and takes no orders from any other country? Do you not think it would be logical in the circumstances to adopt a distinctive national flag?
Personally, I am not in favour of including on the national flag the fleurs-de-lis, to remind us of our ties with France, no more than the union jack to remind us of our ties with England, because new Canadians

could also demand the inclusion of a new element recalling their own country of origin.
If we are all Canadians from sea to sea, we should, I think, in the interest of national unity, adopt an essentially Canadian flag.
In closing my remarks, I should like to refer to part of a talk given by Clement Brown, a newspaperman, and reported in the monthly review Alerte for October and November 1958:
A few years ago, I suggested that the three great physical features of Canada, namely the forest, the prairies and the northern expanses, be represented on our future flag. In terms of colours, that would make it green, gold and white. Other symbolisms might be added: green for our French origins; gold for our British origins; white for the new Canadians; green for our youth as an autonomous nation; gold for our fidelity to the throne; white for the purity of our ideals. The three bands could be either vertical or horizontal, and for colour contrast, the white could be placed between the green and the gold. Some day, I hope that an artist may enable me to see with my own eyes what such a design would look like.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as member for Brome-Missisquoi in the House of Commons, I am convinced of one thing, namely that the people of my riding have entrusted me with the duty of speaking in favour of a distinctive flag.
I am thinking now of a few villages of my constituency, namely that of Foster, where most people are English speaking, while five miles away in the village of St. Etienne de Bolton the people are mostly French speaking.
Mr. Speaker, I can state that, under the present government and the leadership of the Right Honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), a great spirit of national unity pervades the Brome-Missisquoi riding, where people today are anxious to obtain a distinctive flag. Mr. Speaker, even if my late grandmother on my father's side bore the name of Emma Stewart, and her own mother was born overseas, I am convinced that she would object to the terms of the bill now under discussion. I am in favour of the adoption of a flag by the Canadian parliament, by Canadians, for Canadians.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I am being interrupted by members of the opposition, the very ones who want to divide our country in order to rule.
As for me, I am speaking in this house in exactly the same way as in the riding of Brome-Missisquoi and I am sure of one thing: if we had known earlier the spirit of national unity shown by the Prime Minister, it would be much easier for us Canadians to adopt and obtain today a distinctive flag.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to go into the artistic merits of a flag. I only wish to point out that today Canada, our big and young country, does need a distinctive flag.

(Text):
Sir, the other day I was travelling from Ottawa back to my constituency and, as often happens, the subject of a distinctive Canadian flag came up. I came out, as I have always come out, sincerely for a distinctive Canadian flag. I have advocated this ever since I was a young man in high school. I have advocated it in my district, and I have never said different things in different parts of this country. I have always spoken in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. I offered my point of view to my hon. friend, who happened to come from Manitoba and is a member of this house, and I said I had a mandate from my own particular region to speak in this house for a distinctive Canadian flag.
He sincerely put forward the proposition that we are still a young country, that we were brought together by an act of confederation through the efforts of John A. Macdonald and George Etienne Cartier in 1867. He mentioned the fact that we are still a very young country, the fact that we could differ on what should be in a flag and could recognize our differences, that we could really differ and talk about the matter openly without trying to rub the sores of division, as is ofttimes done by hon. members opposite.
I pointed out to him that I felt the time had come for us as Canadians to discuss the desirability of a distinctive Canadian flag.
I am sure of one thing, Mr. Speaker. The debate such as that taking place here in this house this afternoon is helpful, coupled with the fact that national unity has really been underlined by the spirited direction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) today. When he talks about a spirit of Canadianism, he talks about a factor that is truthfully uniting Canadians, a factor that I can tell the people in my riding will bring about a distinctive Canadian flag much faster than would otherwise be the case.
I can also say this, however. Even after listening to my friend speak on the train proceeding from Ottawa to Montreal I am still as convinced as I always have been that the time has come, as I said before, for us to advocate a distinctive Canadian flag.
One of the true things about Conservative principles is that we recognize the fact that local affections spring out into broader affections. Conservatives pay a great deal of attention to local affections. Conservative principles say that our primary affections start in our family, our churches, our towns and spread out to our provinces, our country and to wider associations such as the commonwealth and the United Nations. In short, as I

said, Conservative principles state that our local and family affections form the setting for those broader affections.
Speaking for myself, I may say that I am proud when I see the fleur-de-lis flying in the province of Quebec as representing my province. I am proud of our flag in the province of Quebec. I am also proud when I see the union jack. When I see it flying it says to me that Canada is an equal partner with other nations in the British commonwealth of nations, an association that plays such an important part in the modern world of today.
I am proud when I look at the flag with the fleur-de-lis on it representing my province. I am proud when I look at the union jack which represents our co-equal position in the commonwealth of nations. I would be equally proud to recognize a United Nations flag which represents the important work being done by this great world body. However, I think one thing is missing, namely a flag which represents a real Canadianism, a spirit which prevails from Atlantic to Pacific in this country today.
As a Conservative may I say this. While I have a flag that represents my local loyalties, I should also like to have a distinctive Canadian flag which would represent my loyalty to this country, called Canada in which I live. May I repeat what I have already said. I feel that under the direction this country is getting today from the Prime Minister, we are coming closer, day by day, to attaining just such a distinctive Canadian flag.
I cannot support the bill before us today because, as I said before, I believe that a Canadian flag should be adopted by Canadians for Canadians in the Canadian House of Commons. I recognize the fact that many of my ancestors came from Scotland. However, I do not know whether they, in all seriousness, could support some of the terms of the bill before us. Of one thing I am certain, however. The discussion that has been had this afternoon and the discussions that I am sure will be had in the future on this extremely important subject can do nothing but help in obtaining for the people of Canada something that in my opinion should come very soon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr -Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training and to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs of technical and vocational training undertaken under provincial authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs; to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons; to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council: and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and incidental matters.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Vocational Training AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I feel it is my duty and pleasure to speak on this very important resolution, namely a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training. Perhaps a number of Canadians do not know it, but the federal government has for a number of years been paying part of the cost of vocational schools in the provinces. This additional financial aid will make it possible to do a far better job.
It is interesting to learn that the minister does not intend to depend on immigration as a source of skilled workers as has been done in the past, but rather to train Canadians who are in need of such training. If a proper program had been instituted by the previous government years ago we should not have near the unemployment we have today.
I thank the minister for asking all members to check this resolution and to submit suggestions to help the program. The Progressive Conservative government is to be complimented on this plan to train young Canadians so that they may play a more important part in the building of this great country. As most hon. members know, we have a vocational school in Nanaimo and it is one of the top grade schools in Canada. I have, of course, visited this school many times and I know a number of the fine boys who have graduated and who now hold good positions because of the education and experience gained in this excellent school. Firms in the logging industry know the real value of this school and have placed many of the boys in good positions after they have completed their training. There has always been support for this school from the logging firms operating in British Columbia who realize the value of well trained men. Some of the companies have donated caterpillar tractors, trucks, road graders and other equipment to the Nanaimo vocational training school. This school has been very successful in securing positions for its pupils when they graduate, and I believe the big reason is because of the way the school is operated and because of the system used by Mr. Jack McCreedy under whose able direction the school has operated for many years.
Mr. McCreedy has taken a personal interest in all the pupils and has helped them in many ways. It is my opinion that if all the schools were run in the same efficient manner there would be far less unemployment in Canada. Mr. McCreedy is not at the Nanaimo school at the present time. I understand he is now at the Vancouver vocational training school,
IMr. Speaker.]
but I suggest that if there are to be any factfinding meetings on improvements in vocational training methods Mr. McCreedy should be called in. I am sure his contribution would be a big help to the program the minister has in mind.
I remember that after world war I the government instituted a civil re-establishment program for returned men. While a great many servicemen who took advantage of this plan did benefit from it, many others just wasted their time and the taxpayers' money. It is very important to the success of this new program that proper grades be demanded. Schools that are part of the plan should be carefully checked; they should be required to make sure that the pupils are working and taking every advantage of the opportunity afforded to them. If the federal government is to help finance this program to educate and train young Canadians it should make sure that a good job is being done.
I am very pleased to learn that the plans of the minister include an expanded teacher training program, as we all know that good results from technical and vocational training can only be achieved if there are good teachers. Poor teachers should not be part of this important effort. I think hon. members will all agree that good teachers can do a tremendous job in the training of the youth of Canada and that bad or poor teachers can have a very adverse effect on education. If a teacher is mean and overbearing, if he is overly conceited, he should not be allowed to teach until he is cured of these things that are hard for a pupil to endure.
Look out for the teacher who will not learn. There is a saying that he who graduated yesterday stops learning today is uneducated tomorrow. I feel that is often true of teachers. I will say that in my own constituency and, no doubt, in other constituencies across Canada, there are many fine teachers whose work is undoubtedly of great benefit to our country. I am very thankful that in my youth I had good teachers and they did their best with the material provided. I, of course, went through school as a youth and went through the same troubles that a high-spirited lad goes through today. I had one aunt who claimed that eventually I would be hung. I suppose I was like a lot of young lads, full of life, and I had one of the teachers who taught in my constituency, a Mr. Thomas. I met him a year ago and it was a pleasure to talk to him again, and naturally we talked back to the times when I was a pupil many years ago when I was in school in Victoria.

To give you an idea of how a school teacher can, in certain conditions, help a young fellow out, we were out at recess time and we had some very nice apples, and some of the boys dared me to throw an apple and hit Mr. Thomas. They kept after me and dared me until I agreed to do it. I said to myself: if I throw the apple I will make quite sure I do not hit him. So I threw it way up in the air. Unfortunately, it came down and hit him on the back of the neck. That required that we should go forthwith to the principal's office, and I figured I would come to the usual type of grief-we got the strap in those days and they did not spare it.
The first thing they asked me was why I threw it, and I said I threw it because I had been dared. Then they worked on me and wanted to know who the boy was that dared me, and being a little bull-headed I did not tell them. My reward was that they said I was a very fine boy and loyal to this other young fellow and they would overlook the whole thing. I asked Mr. Thomas, to whom I had not spoken for years, whether he remembered that. He laughed, and said he did remember. I said, you certainly must have loved children to put up with what you put up with in those days, and he said, that is one of the secrets of being a good teacher. I could cite other things along those same lines. When teachers are lacking in these qualities they are going along trying to do a job for our young people without the inspiration which is likely to make it successful.
I might mention another teacher, a Mrs. Bell who was my Sunday school teacher. She was a wonderful influence on my life and for a number of years I could feel that influence. It was quite interesting. A lot of the members here may remember seeing A1 Miller from Toronto on television. He does not know anything about this deal, but it was his grandmother who was such a wonderful influence on me, a boy who according to my aunt might have been hung.
I am very proud of the teachers. I think teaching is one of the most wonderful professions there is in the world. I have spent some money on my daughter teaching her figure skating and she has got on very well. She came home one day and said her instructor, Mr. Albert Enbers, had a contract for her to join Ice Capades. Should she take it, she asked. I said: it is up to you. The next day my daughter came to me and said, would you kindly phone Mr. Enders and tell him I am not going. I am going to go to normal school, I am going to be a school teacher. That was one of the proudest moments of my life. She went to normal school and taught school after that. She gave up a
Vocational Training
very glamourous opportunity to tour the world, you might say, like a good school teacher should.
I should like to ask the minister if consideration will be given to the important matter of the training of musicians. Canadians have contributed greatly to the musical world, and many of our artists have left for other countries to complete their training, and we have lost them.
We have in Nanaimo, the Nanaimo symphony orchestra that has done a wonderful job under the able leadership of Mr. Maurice Kushner. Mr. Kushner is called "Mr. Music of Vancouver island" and has dedicated his life to music. I would ask that some plans be included in the implementation of this resolution to make the training of musicians part of this program.
This represents a most important move on the part of the federal government and one that is long past due. It will encourage and hearten many Canadians who have been waiting for years for such a golden opportunity. Canada is now on the march and years of expansion are ahead. Those who wish to be a part of this great expansion must be well trained, we must have good schools but most important of all they must have good teachers. As I said before, the teaching profession is the most important profession of all and the future of a country in many ways is dependent on good teachers.
I was quite surprised this afternoon when one hon. member who takes as much of the time of the house as he can get, objected to hon. members talking on this resolution. The hon. gentleman's action in making that statement must have required a lot of plain gall. I think it is required when a resolution as important as this one is before us that every sincere hon. member should make a contribution in some way if possible. I do so for the reason that I am interested and also for the reason that we have such a fine vocational school in the city of Nanaimo. It must have made the hon. gentleman very sour to hear hon. members thanking the minister for introducing this important resolution. I have noticed that most hon. members in the house have been taught by their parents to be polite and not to forget their "thank you's". It is a sign of good breeding and hard to forget even though it is distasteful to some people.
I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without offering my hearty congratulations to the minister on the fine work he is doing for Canada at a very difficult time. From all parts of Canada we hear praise of his efforts. The minister is a man who understands the problems of the working man. The minister

Vocational Training
was a working man and a union member before coming to the House of Commons and Canada is very fortunate in having a man of such high calibre as Minister of Labour.
We have just had an example of more rudeness on the part of the hon. member for Timiskaming and even had this comment been intelligible I doubt if it would be worthy of a reply. I wish to close my remarks with a statement attributed to Ben Franklin: Nothing is of more importance for the public welfare than to form and to train up youth in wisdom and virtue. Wise and good men are, in my opinion, the strength of a state far more than riches or arms.

Mr. Chairman, I must first of all congratulate the Minister of Labour on the introduction of this resolution designed to extend the frontiers of knowledge and skill to certain citizens of our country. I take particular pleasure in doing so, as I recall my own active interest in some such measure over a long period of years. Then, too, I am reminded of that tough old pioneer, a constituent of mine, who attending my convention, gave voice to the needs, recognized in part, at least, by this proposed measure. That stalwart citizen of Canada was one of those who share a background not altogether dissimilar to that of the Minister of Labour.
This measure did not form part of our platform in 1958. It is, however, another milestone reaching toward a realization of that greater Canada, the vision of which won for our Prime Minister the confidence and the admiration of the people of Canada. I propose to deal with this matter at some length. In doing so, I make no apology to anyone. This measure represents one of the milestones which characterize so indelibly the difference between the administration that was and the administration that is, and has since 1957 been building and rebuilding the foundations upon which unity and purpose in Canada's national life can be achieved for all Canadians.
If we look back on the days of war we are at once confronted with the inescapable conclusion that the national selective service in those days measured vividly the challenge that would face this nation in the post-war years. Nor need we ever forget the unpreparedness of those days in terms of trained personnel that accentuated the perils of national survival itself. Those were the days when the flags of premonition with regard to the future of Canada's youth and labour force were the unfurling banners of arrogance, indifference and neglect worn by those who today form the official opposition in parliament.

The penalties that are accruing today in terms of unplaced applicants for jobs, in terms of those who search for trained personnel for positions that cannot be filled, in terms of the increasing seriousness of trade imbalance and trade deficit, in terms of the alarming grasp of Canadian resources by foreign capital, all claim the distinction of a common origin. I like to recall the words of Canada's prime minister of those days, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. That oracle of Liberal thought never spoke truer than when he said, "If that new world order is not well on the way before the cease of hostilities, then we may well look for it in vain." I have been told it was the quivering hand of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that held the crystal ball in those days. The pages of Canadian history will always bear the marks of that period, when opportunity to serve the national purpose was looked upon as a stranger by the then government of the day.
The post-war years passed quickly, five, ten, fifteen years. The youth of those days are the untrained unemployed of today. Those were the days when government legislation failed to encourage training necessary to sustain employable people through to the years of maturity. Those were the days when government legislation failed to undertake the tasks of retaining the heritage of Canada's resources for Canadians. Those were the days of budget surpluses so proudly claimed by the Liberal front benches. I say, those surpluses represented and in fact still represent that price which Canadian paid as a first instalment on the anxieties which have been maturing during the past several years.
One need only ask any contractor or any industrial employer to measure the part that untrained and unskilled labour have contributed to the inflationary tendencies which have rocked the very structure of our economic and social life in Canada. Nor has that been the only result. Ask those who have the training; ask those who have the skill. Everyone of them can tell you that he or she has been subsidizing those who through no fault of their own were thrown on the labour market without proper training and, what is worse, without provision for proper training at those times of relaxed labour conditions. Thus was a limitation placed upon their ability to retain and improve their prospects and that of Canada as the years rolled by. The other day in this debate the hon. member for Hull, in referring to this legislation, said:
We recognize that its purpose is to prepare, in a rather distant future, the young generation so that it might play its part within society.

Later on, in the same remarks, he said:
The government has some responsibilities, and it should find the ways and means to relieve the present want while getting ready to give assistance to those who tomorrow will have to change jobs.
This afternoon in the debate the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate remarked: "What about the last three years?" I say to you, sir, and to the members of this house, that if they had been thinking of those people, who tomorrow will have to change their jobs, during the last 22 years, and particularly during the early post-war years, Canada would not be faced with the problem in regard to unemployment that it is facing today. That is one of the reasons why this legislation is needed to alleviate in some measure the situations and conditions which members of the opposition must claim and own as part of the heritage of 22 years of opportunity deferred in the crystal ball of a politician. Do not forget, that it was the quivering hand of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who cradled the crystal ball.
The opposition say that this bill is too modest. We acknowledge that it is modest; we certainly think it is only part-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, unlike most previous speakers, I will not delay the passage of this resolution by congratulating the minister and the government on its introduction. However, with the time at my disposal I want to say a few words in a general way on it, and particularly in so far as it may be applicable to the economic welfare and future of the Atlantic provinces.
At the present time a very large technical institute is under construction in New Brunswick. This institute is being built within the city limits of Moncton and negotations for its erection were conducted in the year 1959 by the former premier of New Brunswick, the present Minister of Forestry. This institute is a start on a new program to train unskilled workers in New Brunswick. It is my hope that

Vocational Training
the new government of New Brunswick will accelerate the existing construction and take steps to establish and construct an additional number of institutes throughout the province.
As we all know, the aeroplane and the car have replaced the buggy; the diesel engine has more or less displaced the steam engine. Centralized traffic control has replaced hand signalling and telegraphic communication on the railways of this country, and more recently the operation of automatic hump yards has replaced marshalling yards at some of our rail centres. We all know that the jet age has already almost outmoded modern postwar aeroplanes.
I mention these few examples to impress upon hon. members that these changes, which are confined to transportation alone, have caused a great deal of displacement and interruption of work for many men throughout the country. Admittedly these improvements were necessary for the progress and expansion of the nation. However, each and every one of these examples of automation in the transportation field has caused a great deal of displacement and in fact unemployment for many trained and unskilled Canadians.
Just before we adjourned for supper the hon. member for Assiniboia said that the minister should have given a fuller explanation at the resolution stage. It is my opinion that the measure was very well introduced by the minister at this stage and not only by the minister but also by the Prime Minister who made reference to this subject during the debate on the speech from the throne. As found on page 44 of Hansard for Monday. November 21, the Prime Minister said:
Then there is vocational training. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said the other day, 40 per cent of the labour force, which includes all of us, did not get beyond elementary school. Many cannot secure jobs because they have not the necessary training.
The Prime Minister went on to elaborate on this aspect of the throne speech.
I should also like to draw the attention of hon. members to the brief presented by the Canadian Legion as recently as October 24 last when representatives of the Legion appeared before the Prime Minister's committee on employment together with representatives of many other segments of the economy. The Legion brief was a very short one and I commend it to all members of the house. It was presented by R. E. MacBeath, third vice president. I am particularly interested in the Legion brief because Mr. MacBeath is a resident of my constituency and a very active supporter of the Legion. On page 2 of the Legion brief there is the following statement which I believe is very appropriate:
[Mr. Creaghan.j
The Canadian Legion believes that the acute unemployment situation which we now face is a temporary one and that the solution to the temporary aspect can be found. We do, however, suggest that measures could be adopted to help protect against recurring unemployment. One such measure would be for the federal government to immediately institute an intensive program of academic and trades training similar to that implemented for veterans of world war II. This would help to relieve some of the immediate problems and would ensure that our citizens were better trained and better qualified for future employment. This would benefit Canada's economy because the more highly trained and proficient our citizens are, the more productive they will be.
I think the Legion brief expresses fairly well the feeling of all members of the house and can be identified with the resolution now under discussion. As far as the maritime provinces and New Brunswick in particular are concerned, if the resolution is acted upon by the people and particularly the provincial governments it will do much to eliminate recurring unemployment. It was about recurring unemployment that Mr. MacBeath was primarily concerned.
The regional director of the unemployment insurance commission issues a press release monthly, I believe, and we all know that in the Atlantic provinces the highest rate of unemployment occurs during the months of February and March. Last February the report of the regional director contained the following as found in an article in the Moncton Transcript of February 12 last:
Once again the unskilled construction worker led the list taking up 19 per cent of the total applicants. Loggers and bushmen were next with 13 per cent, carpenters third with 8 per cent, and taxi, truck and tractor operators had 6 per cent of the total.
These four classifications represented 46 per cent of the total unemployment in the province of New Brunswick last February. It is also pointed out in the article that all but 5 per cent of the applicants were in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. However, 80 per cent of the unemployed people in the province of New Brunswick were males.
The last annual report of the Department of Labour points out that a certain number of personnel in the armed forces and a number of permanent employees of the federal government were given courses under the existing vocational training and technical institute legislation. So far as the armed forces and civil servants were concerned, this aspect of conversion courses or further education was paid for entirely by the federal government. Not only did the government pay all wages involved but also the full amount that the provinces charged for teachers' salaries. It is my hope that from time to time more and more permanent force

personnel and people with permanent employment with the federal and provincial governments will take advantage of these extension courses. We have not heard very much complaint from the provincial ministers of education about the federal government subsidizing this form of education and, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury said earlier today, we have heard no complaints about the fact that the federal government paid the cost of educating so many thousands of veterans after the last war.
One point I should like to bring out is the importance of getting the unemployed and the youth of the country to take advantage of the legislation that we expect will be introduced following the passage of the resolution. This point can be summarized in this way. Too many of the youth of the country are forced to go to work while still in their teens. At the other extreme too many of our older citizens must remain at work, whether at manual labour or otherwise, until well after the age of 65. If it were possible for more of the young to take courses at technical institutes after graduation from elementary school or high school as the case may be and if at the same time it were possible for more of our senior citizens to retire at the age of 65, I think the day would soon arrive when we would not be faced with the threat of recurring unemployment. By inducing people to remain at school or in training at institutes for a longer period of time it will be possible to shorten the working life of the average Canadian. If we can cut a few years off each end it may be possible to reduce unemployment and at the same time to provide better working conditions and job security for those about to be trained.
I hope that the bill will be introduced soon, and that following passage of the bill it will be possible for the government, through the Minister of Labour, to negotiate new vocational and technical training agreements with the provinces of this country. At that time I urge the minister to pay particular attention to the drafting of the agreements. I hope that the new agreements will have a clause to protect against any type of political discrimination, not only for the applicants attempting to enroll in the schools and institutes but also in the construction contracts which will necessarily follow when new technical institutes are being built.
In conclusion, although I omitted it at the opening of my remarks, I want to thank the minister and the government for this most progressive legislation.

speechtext:
It may be true that some members do not go to caucus. However, if the bill is already drafted, then the advantages suggested by Mr. Roberts in having a resolution stage, namely that certain suggestions being made to the cabinet would finally end up in the bill, would appear to be lost in this particular case.
I am pleased to find that the minister has given consideration to the advantages to be derived from this type of legislation. I am only guessing, but I imagine that he is mainly interested in solving the unemployment problem by helping with the re-training of those people who do not have the necessary educational or technical qualifications to take advantage of the job opportunities being offered. I agree that this is probably a very good thing, but it is not necessarily what all the members have been saying in the last several hours. It would seem to me that they have been suggesting that a new system be implemented to replace our educational system which, as some members have suggested, is still in the horse and buggy days or the oxcart stage.
It seems to me there may be some truth in these suggestions. I am surprised to find how unsuitable our educational system is for preparing young people to take their place in life today. Those who have the responsibility for our educational system should be listening to the members tonight. I would think that within a very short time the concept of Canadian education rather than provincial education is going to be popular. This is not a new thought in the vocational and technical training field because there are many members in parliament tonight who have had the benefit of a national education, paid for by the federal government, in schools which were not conducted on a provincial basis. It would seem to me that the training they received under that particular scheme- I refer to the veteran's scheme-was no less acceptable to the country because it was national in scope rather than having taken

Vocational Training
into consideration the oddities and idiosyncrasies that are sometimes apparent in provincial educational schemes.
It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that in looking at our educational program we should decide exactly what we want to get from that program. I think most of us who have teenage children or who have been around teenagers will have been surprised at the age they reach without having decided for themselves what they want to do. In many cases our grandfathers would have been shocked to find these children still interested in getting an allowance from their fathers instead of being out making their own way in life. Our young people in Canada today have the opportunity to obtain an education such as was not available 20 or 30 years ago. However, when these young people complete their education, in many cases they are not much better trained for a vocation than they are when they leave public or elementary school. It seems to me that, whether our students go to a technical school, or any other type of secondary school, when they leave that school they should at least have a well rounded education. They should be able to carry on the day to day business of life in a manner that will protect them from the many pitfalls in our economy today.
If these young people are going to work and buy things on credit, as most people do, then they are going to need an education to protect them from the moneylenders. They are going to have to be able to read, and I do not mean just read the newspapers. They should be able to read newspapers and understand what they say. Even the education provided in a vocational school should be sufficiently well rounded that the students can continue to gain education throughout their life, because this will be vitally necessary in our changing economy. It seems to me that they should receive enough education that they will be versatile.
Training has been given to some people in highly specialized fields such as electronics, telegraphy and other forms of communication, and within a short time their training has become obsolete. We now find that instead of using 10 or 12 people to operate a small relay station, automatic equipment is now used. When something goes wrong, a light goes on 400 or 500 miles away and changes and corrections can be made in those circuits by remote control. No one even needs to go to the station to do some of this maintenance work. Changes of this type make the training in these fields obsolete very quickly.
It seems to me that people who receive training in such fields should also have an academic background which would enable

them to make the transition from one vocation to another in the shortest possible time. One of the things we have to keep in mind is that the Canadian economy itself is demanding this type of training. The training that we are giving to the young people in Canada is not only training that is going to help these young people take their place in the economy, it is also going to help us maintain a well rounded economy.
It seems to me that in Canada we have in many spheres of endeavour neglected to do the training which has been necessary and which would have produced the people who would have been able to fill the jobs that we are continually given to understand can be filled only by imports. I should like to use the example of the trans-Canada pipe line when it went through Canada. Continually in negotiations and discussions with the pipe line company we were faced with the problem of not having high pressure welders that were able to do the job. It was said that these welders had to be brought in from the United States. It was true that we had many welders in Canada but most of them were not trained sufficiently so that they could do the type of work that was necessitated by this type of high pressure pipe line.
It seems obvious that our vocational system in Canada should be training the type of people that are going to be employable not only now but in the future and that part of this technical training for which assistance is given by the federal government should be on a highly developed economic study basis wherein the department studies the needs and the forward trends of vocational training, just as they would in any other field of endeavour, so that we are not training people for engineering jobs in connection with aircraft that will be obsolete before they are through their training or that we are not teaching students radio and electronics in fields that will be obsolete before they have the opportunity of practising in those fields.
If this work is done, it will have to be done by the federal government in the direction that it will give. I am pleased to note that the Minister of Labour is giving consideration to this much wider field. In every riding and in every area of this country I am sure we have and will continue to have a much greater need for vocational training than we have had in the past.
In my own area of northern Ontario we need vocational schools much worse than we need any other type of school. We have many opportunities for employment in many fields of endeavour but in that part of the country we lack the facilities to which to send our children for training. If these facilities were available it would be much easier for our

people to provide their children with the educational background that will afford them the opportunity of obtaining employment in satisfactory jobs for which they are trained and which they are capable of doing.
I hope the minister has given consideration, as has been suggested by many of his backbench members, to this broadening of national education in the technical and vocational fields. Assistance has been given on the college and university levels. Now we are extending the assistance to the technical and vocational training levels. I would suggest that the studies that were made and the records that were kept by the Department of Veterans Affairs, which had considerable interest and experience in this particular field during the war, be examined. I think that such a study will provide the minister and his officials with a great deal of experience which was gained the hard way by them and which should not need to be repeated by the provincial governments in their field of endeavour. Not only do I hope that this bill will be before us shortly, I hope it will have in it those things the minister had in mind in relationship to training because of automation and because of unemployment and I hope the minister will give consideration to the many suggestions which have been made by his own backbenchers and others in this debate and which, in my opinion, would make for a much better national vocational training program.

speechtext:
We have heard this evening from members who have represented various provinces in the dominion. I am the only representative of an extremely important area of Canada and I therefore feel constrained to rise and explain the problems that confront us in connection with vocational training in the Yukon. If there were in the chamber other members from the Yukon I should not be obliged to take this position, even though it may distress the hon. member who has just taken his seat as well as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Vocational training is a particular problem in Yukon. We have none. We have none because of a number of factors, most of which are soluble only through assistance by the federal government. The Yukon simply does not have the revenue with which to support a comprehensive educational system and, as the situation stands, we are heavily subsidized.
The youngsters in the Yukon who wish to take vocational training are now faced with the problem of either going outside-or what we call outside-to areas such as Edmonton or Vancouver and endeavouring to take it there
Vocational Training
or they take advantage of the limited possibilities available for obtaining apprenticeship training under qualified tradesmen in the Yukon itself. Until recently we had never had an accurate survey of the educational problems existing in the Yukon. However, pursuant to a resolution passed by our legislative council last year a committee was set up to investigate all phases of education in the Yukon territory. This report was just published this year. Undoubtedly the minister will be referring to those portions of it dealing with vocational training in the Yukon.
As most hon. members know, the provinces share in vocational training grants provided by the federal government as indicated in the report of the director of Canadian vocational training for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1959. This agreement that is in existence with the provinces provides for the expenditure, over a five-year period that began on April 1, 1957 of $40 million of federal government assistance to the provinces in the building, equipping and operating of vocational and technical schools, institutes and training centres. Of this amount $25 million is provided exclusively for assistance on capital projects, with preference being given to trade and technical institutes or approved vocational high schools. The capital appropriations is allotted to the provinces on the basis of population in the 15-19 year age group. The remaining $15 million is distributed by way of annual allotment to the provinces for sharing the operating costs of similar institutes and schools or, if desired, a province may claim as much as half of its annual allotment against the capital costs of such institutions. The federal allotment for the Yukon is on the whole quite small. In the year 1958-59 it amounted to $21,100. The territory claimed only $3,212.28 of that amount for that year.
I say that the federal government is vitally concerned in financially supporting the vocational educational system in the Yukon. The Yukon did not participate at all in the year 1958-59 in the federal government supported provincial apprenticeship training scheme. That is the scheme wherein the province shares 50-50 with the federal government in the cost of approved plans. The Northwest Territories shared to the extent of $303.81. One wonders why these schemes are not working in the Yukon.
On advice from the Minister of Labour some two years ago I suggested to Yukon educators that we should try to encourage our youngsters to take on job training under this scheme where the territorial government pays 50 per cent of the cost and the federal

Vocational Training
government pays the balance. On fairly extensive inquiry in the territorial government administration, which comes under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, I found that none of them even knew of any agreement with the federal government for implementing this scheme.
I think the statistics indicate that the total amount of assistance which the Yukon can expect at the moment from the federal government in connection with the capital cost of new construction or participation in these trading schemes is not very great. Mr. Ford of the vocational training branch here in Ottawa paid a visit to the Yukon and made a fairly extensive survey of the vocational requirements there. He was of the opinion that there was a real need for a training program which could be provided in part by our high school in Whitehorse and in part by other agencies.
The committee on education which produced its report this year has come up with some interesting statistics in relation to the number of people who could be employed in various trades if they were qualified by vocational training institutes. I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the accuracy of the statistics which the committee has produced is in my view very much in doubt, because while the various trades are listed together with the number of potential employment vacancies it would appear that the statistics themselves are calculated on the basis of an inquiry conducted by education officials in the Yukon in relation to all children who were then attending school and that they did not take into account any children in the age group 15 years and above who were not attending school. These comprise a fairly large group. For instance, most of the Indian youngsters leave school when they reach the age of 15 or 16, and the Indian people in my constituency are important- they comprise between one fifth and one sixth of the total population. So there is a large group here which would find vocational training to be of decided assistance.
I do not intend to go into the question of the advantages of vocational training. The cost of the scheme of vocational training when a building has to be erected would be fairly substantial and the operating loss alone would probably amount to $50,000 a year, but when one reflects on the savings that could be effected in welfare and related payments by producing useful citizens as a result of such training the cost does not appear to be such a great one.
There is another aspect of this question to which I should like to draw the minister's attention. As I have said, all our education in the Yukon is heavily subsidized. Federal participation in the field of education and 
particularly of vocational education in the Yukon requires co-operation between the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in so far as her responsibilities relate to Indian Affairs, as well as the Minister of Labour. All three departments must co-operate if they are to produce a reasonable approach to vocational training in the Yukon.
I have suggested before, and I suggest again, that perhaps one of the methods by which vocational training could be achieved in the Yukon would be to enter into a scheme in co-operation with the territorial administration whereby youths could obtain vocational training on heavy equipment such as draglines, bulldozers, shovels and the like. If an arrangement could be made during the winter season when the bulk of this equipment is not being used, if it could be hired by the educational authorities with funds from a subsidy paid by the Department of Labour, perhaps as an extension of the apprenticeship training scheme, a portion being paid by the territorial government, I think considerable practical benefit would be derived. In this fashion, not only would the equipment be utilized during the off season months but it would be serving a good purpose by producing skilled operators for the construction season ahead.
There is also one further glaring omission in the report by the committee on education, which, by and large, is a very excellent report. That is, that when discussing the trades and the anticipated number of employee vacancies in the various trades miners are not taken into consideration at all. Mining represents our future in the Yukon and there is no reason at all why vocational training or on the job training cannot be offered in this field. There are active mines in the Yukon which are operating all the year round and I am sure that both labour and management would welcome a scheme whereby youngsters could be trained to become skilled miners. There are those who feel that perhaps the heavy equipment which the army uses in the road maintenance program could be utilized for the training of young men. This, of course, would have to be taken up in co-operation with the Minister of National Defence.
I want to deal briefly with the recommendations of the committee because they do involve action by the federal government if they are to be implemented. The main recommendation appears to be that a composite high school should be constructed in the Whitehorse area affording academic as well as vocational training. This is not at all out of line. I think the vocational training needs

of the Yukon could be very ably met by the federal government participating in such a scheme. I am sure that the Indian affairs branch would participate financially depending on the number of Indian children admitted to such an institution and I am sure that other departments of the federal government which have financial responsibilities in the Yukon would also participate.
One last thing which I want to draw to the minister's attention before I resume my seat concerns the vocational training of the young girls in the Yukon. There are many who believe that this field could be very fruitful. There is a large modern hospital in the Yukon where girls can receive training as nurses' aides or even pre-vocational training as laboratory assistants. They could obtain this training in the field of dietetics or even in laboratory work which is not out of reason at all.
I conclude with these few suggestions which I hope the minister will take into consideration and discuss with his colleagues the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I look forward to seeing at least the apprenticeship training aspects of the scheme which will likely be included in the legislation that will follow this resolution somewhat enlarged. I urge the minister to do what he can to see that the territorial administration through his colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources undertakes to activate the apprenticeship training agreement provisions of the existing departmental policy.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Starr thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-49, respecting technical and vocational training assistance.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
