speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment and operation of a national productivity council and the appointment of its members and staff, to define its duties and objects, to authorize it to exercise certain powers and to provide for other related and incidental matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.
Productivity Council

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the conference on unemployment held in Ottawa in October, the Prime Minister suggested the establishment of a national productivity council. His specific proposal, which outlined the need for such a council and the functions it might undertake, was accepted by leaders from commerce, industry, labour, finance and education. Representatives of the various organizations and associations present at the conference agreed in principle that such a council was highly desirable. In making this proposal the Prime Minister stressed the need for the full support and active participation of Canadians in all sectors of the Canadian economy. I should like to outline briefly for the benefit of hon. members the government's thinking and planning respecting the establishment of a national productivity council. The determination to establish such a council is a completely new development for Canada and it pioneers in new fields of Canadian economic development.
While speaking in the budget debate last spring the hon. member for Vancouver Centre suggested the need for this kind of a council and I would like to give him full credit for bringing this important matter to the attention of the house. All of us are justly proud of the fact that Canada takes its place among the forefront of industrial nations. We are recognized as one of the greatest and most successful trading nations. Our citizens enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world. This enviable position can only be maintained, however, if we are willing to take bold and energetic steps in many fields of economic activity.
While speaking in the throne speech debate the Prime Minister mentioned that for a considerable number of years after world war II Canada sold her goods in a sellers' market. Most products were in world short supply and customers from all over the world beat a path to our doorstep asking for our goods on terms which were very favourable to us. In more recent years, however, a very different set of circumstances has prevailed. War devastated countries have rebuilt their economies and are now our competitors rather than our customers. All over the world the competition for markets is extremely keen.
At a time when markets at home and abroad are becoming increasingly competitive it is essential that Canadian industry be as efficient as possible. We believe that this task can best be carried out by enlisting the help of as many people as possible who are concerned with the production and distribution of goods. We are proposing that representatives of commerce, industry, labour, agriculture and other primary industries, government, consumers, professional groups,

Productivity Council
as well as those from other walks of life, should pool their combined knowledge and skills to assist industry in achieving a more effective utilization of Canadian resources.
In essence, this means obtaining the best possible use of all the factors of production and distribution, including capital, materials, plant and machinery, labour and land. In this manner, Canadians can achieve a higher standard of living through a greater and more efficient flow of goods. They will also strengthen Canada's competitive position in both domestic and foreign markets and hence create new and expanding employment opportunities for Canadian workers.
The resolution before the committee is for the establishment of a national productivity council to consist of 25 members. Five members will represent industry and commerce, five will be drawn from organized labour, five will come from agriculture and other primary industries, five will be appointed from the general public, and four will be technically qualified persons from scientific departments of government. The twenty fifth member of the council will be the executive director who will be responsible for implementing the work of the council. The government will ask leaders from each of the fields mentioned to serve on the council for periods of up to three years. It is the government's view that appointment to the council should be regarded as an opportunity to serve Canada in a task of the utmost importance, one on which the government places the highest priority.
The policies of the council will be implemented through a small highly qualified staff. The objects of the council are to foster and promote the development of improved production and distribution methods; the development of improved management techniques; the maintenance of good human relations in industry; the use of training programs at all levels of industry; the use of retraining programs to meet changing manpower requirements; the extension of applied industrial research; and the dissemination of technical information.
The council will be financed through grants from the federal government amounting to approximately $150,000 each year. We are hopeful, however, that non-governmental interests will also assist in financing the work of the council. The government will make an additional contribution to match all private financing.
Obviously the council and its small staff cannot accomplish this great task without additional help. It is intended, therefore, that a great deal of the actual implementation of the productivity program should be carried

out by the interests represented on the council. Regional, area, and industry teams and committees should be organized to carry the work of the council to all parts of Canada and into all industries. Local productivity committees should be formed on an area basis, and industry committees on an industry basis.
The national council should act as a policy making body and should assist in the establishment of regional and industry productivity committees. Its chief objective should be to develop and maintain in the various and changing circumstances of industrial life a positive attitude of mind in industry, among both management and labour, respecting industrial efficiency.
It may be of interest to hon. members to hear a little about the experience of other countries in the field of productivity. Productivity councils have been very successful, both in the United Kingdom and in Europe, as instruments in raising industrial efficiency. While the Canadian council must, of course, design its activities to suit and conform to Canadian conditions, I believe that the experience of the British and Europeans in this field can be a very useful guide to us.
In the immediate post-war period industry in Europe and in the United Kingdom realized the essential importance of increased productivity if it was to regain its position in an era of rapid technological change. Therefore, in 1948 an Anglo-American council on productivity was formed, so that the technical information and experience of United States industry could be placed at the disposal of industry in the United Kingdom. The Anglo-American productivity council was a successful experiment. When its activities came to an end, the British productivity council was formed in 1952. Its members are elected from personnel nominated by the constituent organizations of the council. These organizations are the British employers confederation; federation of British industries; the trade union congress; the association of British chambers of commerce; the national union of manufacturers; and the nationalized industries. Representatives of both management and labour are, therefore, working together with the common aim of increasing productive efficiency in industry as a whole.
When the British council was formed it had as a guide three lessons derived from the experience and operations of its predecessor, the Anglo-American council on productivity. The first was that the major influence which such an organization could exert was on the climate of opinion about productivity. The second was that joint study of industrial problems by people drawn from all levels of industry was the way to a more positive

approach to these problems. The third lesson was that there was a wide and rapid spread of knowledge about industrial techniques and equipment in the United States, and a strong determination to submit every existing practice to continuous critical examination.
With these guiding principles in mind the council decided that the aim of creating a wider appreciation for the need of higher productivity, and of the methods that lead to it, could be carried out only by enlisting the help of as many people actually engaged in industry as possible. To this end local productivity committees or associations were established. These local committees are composed of representatives from both labour and management, from all levels of industry, and representatives of professional bodies and technical education. Their task is to spread more widely knowledge of the best industrial methods and practices. The means used include inter-factory visits, discussion groups, lectures, conferences, films, courses, seminars in work study and other such techniques. One particularly important aspect of the British productivity council's approach to its work has been stressed: that is in connection with every industrial technique that is considered and every subject discussed the council lays great stress upon the problems of human relations to which any industrial change may give rise.
I have outlined the United Kingdom's approach to the subject in some detail, Mr. Chairman, because the British council is recognized to have made a very significant contribution to the improvement of British industry. But I should also mention that similar activities are carried out in practically every European country. Many of these countries have national productivity centres of their own which have developed national productivity programs to increase industrial efficiency.
In 1953 the organization for European economic co-operation established the European productivity agency. Every important trading country in Europe is a member of this agency and Canada and the United States are associate members. The agency acts as an international co-ordinating centre for national productivity programs and serves as a clearing house for the exchange of information and ideas. It also serves as a laboratory in which new ideas are developed and fed to the national centres.
Productivity centres are not confined to Europe alone. Asia, India, Pakistan, Japan, Iran, Lebanon and the Philippines all have productivity councils or similar bodies whose main function is devising means of increasing national levels of productive efficiency. In
Productivity Council
the western hemisphere there are active programs for increasing productivity in a number of countries including the United States, Chile, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mexico and Panama.
In view of the progress made by other countries in the field of productivity, Canada cannot ignore this field of endeavour. We have, therefore, taken the appropriate steps to launch a national productivity program, to be carried on by the citizens of Canada for the benefit of all Canadians.
As in the other countries where these councils have been so successfully used I am convinced that we in Canada can achieve equally successful results if governments, management and labour will co-operate fully to make Canadian products competitive in both quality and price. On behalf of the government we pledge our full co-operation and effort to achieve this end. We are asking for the full co-operation of Canadian management and labour. On our combined efforts will depend the competitive position of our products, and hence the job opportunities for Canadians in the future.
I think it is clear to everyone that if our products are competitive, as to both price and quality, with goods produced in other countries they will be sold, and Canadians will be employed producing more of them. If they are not competitive, the reverse will be the case. It is up to all of us to see that our products are competitive, so that our people can be employed producing them.
We must all realize that there is no sentiment in the buying habits of the average Canadian, or the citizens of any other country. A housewife or a purchasing agent will buy the best product at the lowest price, no matter where the goods are produced. If Canadian goods are to sell against competition they must be either better quality at the same price, or equal quality at a lower price. I think it is obvious, therefore, that if we are to continue to have high employment in Canada we must make sure that our products are competitive in both quality and price. Prosperity and employment are everybody's business.
I think it has become clear that close cooperation between government, industry and labour will be necessary if Canada is to retain and improve her competitive position both in the home market and abroad. The national productivity council will be an important first step in this direction. What the countries of Europe have done in this regard, we can, and must match and better here in Canada.

Productivity Council
We pledge an all-out effort by the government in this regard. We ask the same cooperation and effort from industry and labour. I feel sure we will receive it.
If we can achieve the same team work effort which our competitors in Europe have achieved our products will become more competitive in both quality and price; we will win a larger share of both the home and the export market, and we will move steadily forward toward our goal of a good job for every Canadian.

Be that as it may, I did want to express personal good wishes to the minister for happiness in his new portfolio. I have other views about his economic outlook and some of the policies he may bring forward but those will be expressed from time to time and all in due course. It would not be fitting for me to dwell on the brevity with which I hope his tenure in his new portfolio will be blessed.
In presenting the resolution to the house the minister referred very correctly to the Prime Minister's announcements of last October 25 and 26 as they appeared in the press at the conclusion of the day and a half conference of leaders of industry and representatives of labour to discuss certain matters with the government on unemployment, a conference well advertised beforehand and while in progress. In any event, the conference was short and since it was not open to the general public I was not there. I do not know what took place. However, I was rather amazed to hear the minister refer to the attitude of certain leaders of industry at that conference when there is nothing on record to show whether or not this

is their true position. Indeed, some of them are on record as having quite the opposite view.
In any event, the announcement of the Prime Minister at the conclusion of the conference that a productivity council would be established was followed by the reference in the speech from the throne to the setting up of such a council and now by this resolution asking leave of the house to introduce a measure to achieve this objective. In his remarks at that time the Prime Minister said, and I think I am quoting accurately, that the Canadian productivity council would be modelled on the United Kingdom productivity council. Then he went on to set out the aims of the Canadian counterpart. I noticed that the minister was much more careful in that regard and apparently had taken the precaution to find out something about the British productivity council. For that I think the house should be grateful because the United Kingdom productivity council, as I hope to show in a moment or two, was established for another purpose and while it is a very good council for the purpose for which it was set up obviously it will not meet the needs that require to be met by a Canadian productivity council. I think the minister will agree with me on that.
I was interested to hear the minister point out the change in circumstances that has taken place over the last number of years from the period of time when we were producing goods to meet shortages and there was a general atmosphere of world shortage in many lines to a period now of high world production and very keen competition. These changed circumstances have come about surprisingly quickly and have presented many very real problems to the government. I hope the minister will proceed to meet these problems and will not tend to minimize them as some of his colleagues have sought to do over the last two or three years.
The genesis of the United Kingdom productivity council was described by the minister. It originated in the Anglo-American council on production formed in 1948 which was followed by the formation of the present council in 1952. It is rather interesting and worth mentioning that the Anglo-American council on productivity was formed at a time when Mr. Paul Hoffman of the United States was heading up the United States Marshall aid program and so much was being done in the world through that program to increase productivity for the purpose of meeting shortages. The point I wish to make is that its purpose was to meet shortages and that was the genesis of the British productivity council.

I think it would perhaps be helpful to the committee in dealing with the resolution and matters that will arise at later stages when the bill is before us if I were to place on record some of the things that the British productivity council will not do. What I wish to put forward in this connection is found in a memorandum submitted by the British productivity council to the select committee on estimates of the United Kingdom parliament on May 25 of this year. One paragraph in the submission is devoted to matters outside the council's scope and I should like to quote a part of paragraph No. 23 in the submission. It reads as follows:
To circumscribe more clearly the area which is the council's chosen field of work, and also to remove possible misunderstandings, it may be as well to state some of the things the council does not do. It does not carry out research; it sees its task as to spread understanding of better methods, as tested and proved in the practice of progressive firms. It does not teach; it believes that this role can be carried out only by educational bodies, and in particular technical colleges, but that much remains to be done to awaken interest in the training they do or could provide. It does not maintain a consultancy service; there are obvious reasons why a joint body could not become involved in individual applications that affected earnings and conditions of work. It does not deal with the division of the fruits of higher productivity; the council believes that all in the nation will benefit from rising productivity, but that individual cases must be left to the normal system of industrial negotiation. It has no views to put forward on national economic policy-
So much for the British productivity council. I noted what I would regard as a discrepancy between the remarks of the Prime Minister on this subject as found in the press releases of that time and the minister's remarks today. If I am right in saying that there is a discrepancy I hope that discrepancy is accounted for by a thorough understanding of what the British productivity council is and an attempt to make the Canadian productivity council of such a nature as to meet our Canadian needs at this time and in the years that lie ahead.
The minister's remarks also interested me for other reasons. He quoted, as I said, the approval of leaders of industry. I happen to have noted a comment of a man in the Financial Post of November 12, 1960, that man being Mr. E. P. Taylor whom I think most hon. members would regard as a man having something, in fact a great deal, to do with industry in this country. In commenting on the Prime Minister's announcement Mr. Taylor had this to say:
In my view, this country has in store for it a long period of slackness in many lines of business and industry, with consequent large scale unemployment and a continuing diminution in the flow of desirable immigrants, unless we face up to the situation and adopt new policies and practices. The answers to our problems will not come as the result of the appointment of advisory bodies
Productivity Council
to the government composed of many people of largely divergent views such as the newly announced productivity council.
I hope the minister will take note of that comment. I hope that this is not an indication of an attitude on the part of the government that the problems to be met can be put aside or sidetracked through this council and that the government ean thereby escape responsibility for the wrong economic policies which they may have pursued in the past three years and for not adopting other economic policies to meet the new conditions which exist in economic fields today.
In that latter connection I must express regret to the minister that the government has seen fit to discontinue the practice of providing confidential information through the preparation of the Economic Outlook, the type of confidential data upon which the government can base its policies. This is a decision that is tragic if viewed objectively by anyone seeking to concern himself with the advancement of the best possible policies. The minister, before he has been in the department many months, will regret the action that was taken before he came to that portfolio, to cut him off from the benefit of information that can be gathered so well in these reports. It is the type of information he will need and upon which he can base policy. However, that is an aside and is not wholly germane to this issue.
The minister went on, in dealing with the development of this council to suit Canadian conditions, to say a great deal about the type of problem that industry, and particularly the export industry has to face in world competition. In that connection I am glad to see that the government is finally recognizing this problem of changes which are taking place so very rapidly in world trading conditions and world economic conditions. They are going on at a pace that makes it difficult to keep abreast of them. I am one who has been very critical of the government for its failure to keep abreast of these world conditions. I hope this indicates the government is now admitting the rapidity of the changes and attempting to deal with them.
I could not help but recall, as the minister was outlining these problems, how many times they had been asserted by the opposition during the last two sessions of parliament, and particularly in the last session, and were scoffed at by the government. I took the trouble of looking up something which I noticed myself during the debate on May 23 of this year in this House of Commons. It will be noted that this was two days before the United Kingdom productivity council was presenting its submission to the estimates

Productivity Council
committee of the United Kingdom government. A supply motion was called on that day and the hon. member for Essex East, my deskmate, moved an amendment which I think should be put on the record. It was part of the 1958 program of the Liberal party, and based particularly on a paragraph having to do with what was then called the Pearson plan. I think I ought to read that amendment. It will be found on page 4142 of Hansard for May 23, 1960:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house recommends for the consideration of the government the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives of governments, industry, labour, agriculture and universities, for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment."
The speech delivered by the hon. member for Essex East during that debate was a very good one and had a tremendous effect it now seems on the government, although it did not seem so on that occasion. At that time the Minister of Labour replied to the hon. member for Essex East and his thesis was that there was no unemployment in Canada and no threat of unemployment. He has since changed that tune or it was changed in a television broadcast by the Prime Minister early in October. However, he went on to discuss this matter more specifically, and in the course of discussing it he said that it was actually what the opposition had suggested on March 2, 1960, and that was right. In the course of a rather able speech on that date on the severe unemployment conditions the hon. member for Laurier set out 25 points to meet some of the economic and unemployment problems of this country and which the minister sought to belittle.
Then, at page 4162 of Hansard for the same date, the minister is reported as saying:
Now they come back with the same suggestion. They have nothing new to offer.
Here we were trying to point out the problem and we are told we have nothing new to offer. Then the minister goes on to give us a little lecture on the setting up of such committees, national advisory committees or productivity councils composed of these representatives of industry, labour, agriculture, universities and so on. He said:
That is one way of shirking the responsibility of government. This government does not intend to set up committees in order to shirk its responsibilities. This government feels it has a responsibility toward this problem, and intends to take action in order to do everything possible to relieve the problem.

That is what we find in Hansard when we read his speech. Then, of all things, the minister was interrupted by his colleague, the Minister of Finance, and he continues:
I know that the setting up of such a large and unwieldy committee is a technique often used by governments that wish to evade their responsibility but, as I said earlier, this government does not intend to evade its responsibility. This government intends to continue to deal with the things for which it is responsible.
You will note that in that paragraph the minister makes it quite clear that he considers that the setting up of a committee or council would be an evasion of the responsibility of government. I do not share his view on that subject and I am happy to see that, at long last, the government has come around to a more sensible view. I do not know whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce persuaded the Minister of Labour to see the light on this subject or just how the change was made. It is not my good fortune to be watching when cabinet meetings are taking place. I do not know just how the change was brought about.
Certainly, the position of the Minister of Labour who spoke for the government on that occasion was a shocking position for the government to take, and one which showed a complete unawareness of the problems confronting the government. I am glad to see that position is now being repudiated, if it is being repudiated. Of course, if it is not being repudiated by this measure we have no collective responsibility of the cabinet, and one of the ministers should resign but which one is not clear. I hope, therefore, that this means repudiation of the policy laid down by the Minister of Labour.
It could be, however, that the Prime Minister settled the issue because he made his announcement outside the house right after the conference on unemployment. There were no cabinet meetings between the time of the conference on unemployment and the announcement by the Prime Minister, so perhaps it is not a cabinet decision and that is how it was done. In any event, it is of small consequence, however it is done, as long as the cabinet is now repudiating the Minister of Labour and his whole wrong view.
There are a good many questions that could be asked about certain areas that are intended or not intended to be covered by the bill. But for my part I take the view that the economy of the country is in an extremely serious situation at the moment and that the Prime Minister's announced reason for calling this session in order to deal with some of these problems of consequence was a proper one. I have taken the view that if

the government has legislation to bring forward in order to meet these problems I for one want to see that legislation and to approve it or reject it, as I see fit, when I see it. However, I should like to see it and I want it brought forward for that purpose.
After all, at this resolution stage we are merely deciding whether the government shall have leave or permission to bring in legislation on this subject. I think there is no doubt that it should have that permission. I should like to see the legislation as soon as possible and I should like to get forward with the discussion of that legislation when it can be properly examined by the house and, I hope, improved if it needs improving. If it is perfect in the form in which it is introduced, so much the better. However, I hope the minister will not share the view of his colleague the Minister of Justice, namely that all legislation brought in by the government is perfect. I hope he will have an open mind when we come to the later stages and have the actual bill before us. For that reason I propose to conclude my remarks now and, as far as I am concerned, to allow the minister to bring forward his legislation in order that we may see it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have just a few comments to make and perhaps I may not even have time to do that, I observe on looking at the clock. In any event, may I say that I listened intently to the introductory remarks of the minister because, as he himself said, this is a sort of new departure in Canadian governmental activities. We are also interested in what its end result might be with regard to our economy and the people who are unemployed.
I hope the minister will excuse me if once in a while I refer to him as the minister of transport; this tendency still exists. He seems not to fit quite properly in his present portfolio. However, I am sure he will give a good account of himself just as he did when he was minister of transport.
I hope that we are not perhaps embarking on another miniature throne speech debate. However, I am quite sure that this is a matter of such great importance that a number of members in the House of Commons will want to express their views on it. If what happened today is any indication of what will happen in the future, I am quite sure that they will take advantage of that opportunity. This may prevent the attainment of the objective or the expressed desire of the hon. member who just sat down to have the bill introduced at the earliest possible moment.
While the minister in his introductory remarks went into some detail or gave an explanation of sorts as to the structure and
Productivity Council
composition of the national productivity council, in my opinion it was unfortunately still rather vague. Because of the vagueness of the explanation one is prevented from putting his hand out and saying, We will endorse wholeheartedly whatever project the minister has in mind. As I have said, the explanations were not in sufficient detail to allow outright endorsation without knowing just exactly what we are endorsing.
In my opinion, this is unfortunately a bad practice that is developing in the resolution stage preceding money bills in that the ministerial explanations or introductions ofttimes are excessively brief and one sometimes feels that he is buying a pig in a poke. I am not particularly critical of the minister in this instance or more critical of him than I am of any of his colleagues who engage in the same sort of thing. But perhaps if some detailed explanation had been given one would be able to form a better opinion as to whether this particular resolution should be accepted at all. As the matter stands, we are not sure as to just what is contained in it.
While the minister was speaking a number of things cropped up in my mind in connection with the details as to how this productivity council would function and what would be its policy. I think these are important questions to which there should be answers before we come to any conclusion as to whether it is a good thing or whether it will accomplish what the government says it hopes it will accomplish. For instance, there is no indication as to how often the productivity council will meet, or whether it will have within itself authority to break up into subgroups or subcommittees in order to look at specific sections of the economy. There is no indication of the form of the reports. Will there be reports? Will there be recommendations? If so, to whom do the recommendations go? Do they go to the government or do they go to the industries? Do they go to the agriculture department if they are concerned with that section? Are the reports or recommendations, if there are to be any, to be public or are they to be secret? I think these are legitimate questions.
As to the so-called secretariat that will perhaps administer or institute the ideas on policies of the council, what is it to consist of? I understood the minister to say that it was to consist of experts. Are these to be people in the field of economics or in the field of administration or are they to be technical people or who are they to be? This is an extremely important factor. The minister announced small groups on a provincial and local basis of some sort. What is their relationship with the council? Lack of information on these matters to a degree

Business of the House prevents one from saying at this stage, at any rate, in a blindfolded way that we endorse or that we will not endorse a particular idea. If I might be permitted to do so, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could call it ten o'clock and continue tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow the first item will be second reading of the bill pertaining to technical and vocational training. If that business is completed it will be followed by discussion of the resolution which is now before us on the productivity council. That business will hold true for Friday-I refer to those two items-if not completed on Wednesday, followed by item No. 7 on today's order paper, namely the resolution dealing with amendments to the Pension Act.

May I just ask the house leader to clarify one point in his remarks. In the event of this resolution being disposed of tomorrow would the second reading stage of the bill precede the Pension Act resolution on Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There may be some adjustment in the program I have outlined. If so, I will announce it tomorrow. In case there is a change-and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has suggested to me a possible change-we might have the reverse order and put the pension resolution on the program on Friday before anything else. If any spare time develops on Wednesday or Friday, and these items happen to pass, we would proceed with the setting up of some of the special committees that I have announced on previous occasions. Thursday will be a private members' day.

maintopic: U-2 FLIGHTS    USE OF CANADIAN FACILITIES BY U.S.
U-2 FLIGHTS    USE OF CANADIAN FACILITIES BY U.S.
speechtext:
1.	Has the minister of external affairs or the government received any reports since May, 1960 of United States U-2 aircraft flying over Canadian territory?
2.	If so, what has been the purpose of such flights?
3.	Has the Canadian government taken any steps to reach an agreement with the United States government regarding the use of Canadian air bases and/or Canadian air space by United States aircraft, similar to the agreement recently reached between Great Britain and the United States?
4.	If so, what progress has been made toward an agreement?
Answer by: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary
of Slate for External Affairs):
Question
1.	Yes. Since May, 1960 requests for two flights were made in accordance with agreed procedures and arrangements for the flights of all United States service aircraft over Canada.
2.	These requests were similar to requests made for earlier flights of such aircraft referred to in a statement made in the House of Commons by the Acting Prime Minister on May 11, 1960.
3.	Flights of United States service aircraft into and over Canada are conducted in accordance with the regulations contained in P.C. 2307 of April 17, 1952. As the announcement made by Prime Minister Macmillan did not give details of the arrangements governing the use by the United States of bases in the United Kingdom, it is not possible to state whether these arrangements are similar to those applied to United States service aircraft flying over Canada.
4.	Answered by 3.



Wednesday, December 7, 1960
